articles.title: Haven’t received any proposal to join NDA: Supriya Sule
articles.summary: Supriya Sule rules out merger of NCP factions, says talks ended after Ajit Pawar’s death; denies NDA join talks; comments on delimitation proposal.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Even as deputy chief minister Sunetra Pawar called on chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Saturday amid continuing speculation about the merger of the two NCP parties, working president of the NCP SP Supriya Sule categorically ruled out the possibility.She reiterated that this issue had reached a full stop the day her cousin, former deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar, was killed in an air crash this Jan.“I am saying this for the final time. When my brother was alive, there were talks on a merger and a date had been fixed. The day he passed away -- in my mind and within our party -- there was a full-stop to this,” she said.She clarified that she had not received any proposal regarding the merger from the NCP. “I have not received any proposal by phone, WhatsApp, letter or any other means of communication,” she said.Responding to media questions on whether the NCP (SP) is considering joining the NDA alliance, she said, “There are no such talks. A full-stop can be spoken of only if talks are on.”Regarding her meetings with NCP leader Praful Patel in recent days, she said the two families have known each other for decades and that both of them were part of several parliamentary committees. “We meet regularly in the parliamentary committee on finance and FCRA. He was among the invitees for my daughter’s wedding,” said Sule.When asked about her response to Shiv Sena (UBT)’s Sanjay Raut’s comment that talk of the merger was a myth and would fade in the next two days, she said, “He is like an elder brother to me and a senior leader in the MVA alliance. He has the right to say what he wants.”On the NCP (SP)’s possible support for the Centre’s delimitation bill, Sule said, “Six months ago, they had discussed this with several leaders of the INDIA bloc including me and Shiv Sena (UBT)’s Arvind Sawant. We felt that if the seats in all parliamentary constituencies uniformly rise by 50%, then there is no harm discussing this. The size of the electorate in each parliamentary constituency has risen from 13-14 lakh to 25-30 lakh and it is difficult for MPs to reach out to the entire constituency,” she saidHowever, she added, “There is no proposal before us at the moment. articles.title: Wales fans rejoice after win over New Zealand in Cardiff
articles.summary: Steve Tandy's side break a 34-match losing streak against the All Blacks that dates back to 1953.
articles.body:
Welsh rugby fans were "fizzing off their heads" on Saturday night after ending 73 years of hurt against New Zealand in an epic Nations Championship encounter.

The match at the Principality Stadium ended 35-28 to the hosts as the All Blacks' run of 34 successive victories against Wales - dating back to 1953 - came to a juddering halt in Cardiff.

Wales fans were left stunned by a result that came just a week on from having to grind out a win against Japan.

The Prince of Wales, who is patron of the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) also congratulated the team on the win, saying it was a "fantastic result".

Three times Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time in history they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game.

But the approach backfired spectacularly after a brilliant performance sparked astonishing scenes in Cardiff .

A crowd of 55,152 could scarcely believe what had unfolded, and there were scenes of wild celebration with players in tears as Wales began taking in arguably the most famous win of their 145-year Test match history.

Prince William shared a post on Instagram saying it was a "fantastic result by the Wales rugby team".

"My congratulations to the players, coaches and everyone who played a part - you have given fans across Wales a day they will never forget".

Celebrities and politicians were also quick to pay tribute to the team for their heroics on the field.

Speaking on 5Live Breakfast on Sunday morning , First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "Yesterday, meant a heck of a lot to us.

"We are a pretty sporting mad nation. Rugby is very important to us as a nation.

"The fixture against New Zealand is a particularly important fixture. We are a smallish country but in the rugby world, we are the biggest powers.

He continued that "73 years we have failed to beat them, we have come close".

"I have watched Wales come close some 20 years or so ago but sport is wonderful and awful at the same time. It became this psychological block.

"Well, no more. That is it, we can go forward now with a new generation knowing that we can beat New Zealand."

He said the crowd on Saturday "wasn't the biggest, but no doubt that changes".

"I full expect the game next week to be a sell out."

Gavin and Stacey star Jones shared her sheer delight in an Instagram video, with the actor looked visibly stunned following the incredible win over New Zealand.

"This has been decades in the making. Huge congratulations to you all," he wrote on Facebook.

Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said he managed to watch the final part of the game after speaking at the Welsh Labour conference in Llandudno.

"After 73 years we've finally beaten the All Blacks! Can barely believe what I've just witnessed," he said.

John Jenkins was eight-years old the last time Wales beat New Zealand, and without a TV, he was not able to watch the game.

Now 81, he has seen his team beat the All Blacks.

John, who now lives in Shropshire but travels for every match, said he has been present at all of the big occasions in Welsh rugby, and Wales' win against New Zealand was the "most memorable".

"I'm not a gambling man, and if I'd known how to place a bet, I would have bet on Wales because I had this gut feeling that we were going to win.

"Everybody in the last 20 minutes was so anxious," he said.

His daughter Hannah, 50, who also travels to every match despite living in Chichester, said "it felt like a party in the first half, we couldn't quite believe what was happening".

John said: "For 10 minutes after the final whistle, Hannah was sobbing on my shoulder."

Hannah said: "For me and dad to be able to go and watch it together, I keep thinking about turning and looking at his face after we scored the first try - we were just kind of incredulous."

A couple celebrating their wedding day had to delay the speeches by 15 minutes as their guests had to see out the game.

Photographer Rhian Jones, 32, from Ammanford, who captured the celebrations, said the "entirety of the wedding breakfast were on their phones".

"The atmosphere was just so intense, people were screaming, it was incredible and everyone was on edge.

"The bride actually said she felt such a pressure because she was so scared that they were going to lose on her wedding day and obviously it would have dampened the spirit, but of course we didn't," she said.

"We celebrated the couple, celebrated the victory and it was incredible."

She added none of the guests at the wedding in Carmarthen had seen that in their lifetime.

"I tried to edit during the wedding breakfast but I didn't edit anything and I just sat on there with the saxophonist and videographer watching my phone which is very unprofessional, but what are you going to do when it's making history.

"I can't wait to tell my children, and certainly they will be telling their children this in years to come."

Kyle Aston said his 102-year-old granddad had always been a huge rugby fan and was 29 when Wales last beat the All Blacks.

"It would take the long painful wait of 73 years until victory was ours once again, but unfortunately he got tired of waiting and fell asleep just before the full-time whistle," he said.

"Sharing that moment with my grandfather is something I'll never forget.

"Fortunately we are able to watch things back theses days so at some point we will relive the biggest rugby win of our life time."

Warren Atkins from The Cottage pub on St Mary's Street in Cardiff said they were already packed but it was "next level" afterwards.

"We were quite busy before the game but then during the end of the game and after the game it was a different kettle of fish.

He added that the performance was a "promising start" for Wales, and was getting in more beer for next week's game.

"I think we need to step it up a notch again next week seeing how busy it was this week.

"We were expecting busy but you can never prepare yourself for what's to come."

Darren Williams lives abroad but comes home once a year to visit his family in Wales.

He came to Caernarfon Rugby Club to watch the match and said the result was "excellent".

"I hope they can continue like this and keep moving forward," he said.

"The atmosphere was excellent and very enthusiastic."

Daron Owens said she was "really glad" to be at the rugby club to witness such a brilliant performance.

"It was great to see everyone so proud. Everyone was cheering so loudly, it was a really positive place to be."

One fan pitch side at Principality Stadium said they had waited "73 years to be at this game", adding that they were in "total shock but absolutely delighted".

articles.title: Enem 2026 no Amazonas: amigos se unem para conquistar vaga | G1
articles.standfirst: Grupo, que já participou do exame como treineiro, dividiu a rotina com simulados. Os planos futuros incluem cursos de Educação Física, Psicologia e tecnologia.
articles.summary: Estudantes de Manaus compartilham rotina de revisões para o Enem 2026 no Amazonas, focando em vagas para cursos de tecnologia, psicologia e educação física.
articles.body:
Alunos do ensino técnico apostam em preparação conjunta para conquistar vagas no ensino superior em Manaus. — Foto: Lucas Macedo/g1 AM

Quatro amigos que cursam o ensino técnico em Manaus decidiram enfrentar juntos o desafio de conquistar uma vaga na universidade. André Santos, de 17 anos; Cauã Soares, de 17; João Pedro Gomes de Carvalho, de 17; e Felipe Almeida, de 18, fizeram o segundo dia de provas do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) neste domingo (15), depois de um ano de preparação entre aulas, estágios e estudos em grupo.

Os jovens estudam no Instituto Federal do Amazonas ( Ifam ) e no Centro de Educação de Tempo Integral (Ceti). Ao longo do ano, eles dividiram a rotina escolar com simulados e revisões, principalmente de conteúdos que consideravam mais difíceis.

Os quatro já haviam participado de edições anteriores do Enem como treineiros, quando o estudante faz a prova para testar os conhecimentos antes de concluir o ensino médio. Para Cauã Soares, a experiência e a preparação conjunta ajudaram a chegar mais confiantes nesta edição.

"A expectativa é muito boa, a gente treinou o ano todo para fazer essa prova. Graças a Deus, a gente conseguiu se sair bem nos últimos três anos, a gente veio treinando, fez no segundo ano também o Enem. E agora a expectativa é muito alta para ver se a gente consegue fazer os cursos que a gente pensa, o curso que a gente almeja", destacou Cauã.

Durante a preparação, o grupo deu atenção especial à redação e às questões de exatas. A formação técnica também ajudou os estudantes a lidar com conteúdos de algumas áreas cobradas no exame.

Mesmo com a expectativa pela prova e a pressão para conseguir uma vaga no ensino superior, os amigos dizem que a experiência dos anos anteriores ajudou a controlar o nervosismo.

Cada um também já tem planos para o futuro. Entre os cursos desejados estão Educação Física, Psicologia e graduações ligadas à tecnologia.

Para André Santos, de 17 anos, que também participou de edições anteriores como treineiro, a preparação ao longo do tempo tornou a prova menos difícil de enfrentar.

"Desde o ano passado, eu acho que eu vim me preparando cada vez mais e consigo entender um pouco melhor, ficar mais fácil, né, esse ano", avalia André.

Cerca de 114 mil estudantes estão inscritos no Enem 2026 no Amazonas. O segundo dia de provas é realizado neste domingo (15), com questões de Ciências da Natureza e Matemática.

Em Manaus, os portões dos locais de prova abriram às 11h e fecham pontualmente ao meio-dia, seguindo o horário local. A aplicação começa às 12h30. Os horários são os mesmos do primeiro dia do exame.

Neste domingo, os candidatos respondem a 90 questões de múltipla escolha, divididas em duas áreas do conhecimento:

Ciências da Natureza e suas Tecnologias: 45 questões de Biologia, Física e Química;

Matemática e suas Tecnologias: 45 questões.

A duração regular da prova é de cinco horas. Diferentemente do primeiro dia, não há aplicação de redação.

articles.title: 20 Years of Al Jazeera English: The Counter Narrative
articles.summary: Two decades of AJE: Shaping media, amplifying unheard voices and driving global conversations.
articles.body:
Two decades of AJE: Shaping media, amplifying unheard voices and driving global conversations.

In November 2006, Al Jazeera English went live with an audacious mandate: to challenge the traditional hegemony of Western media conglomerates and structurally invert the global news flow by providing a localised, uncompromising perspective from the Global South to the English-speaking world. To mark its 20th anniversary, this documentary delivers a definitive, multilayered chronicle of AJE’s trajectory from a disruptive alternative to dominant Western news media to the globally consumed news source it is today. The film seamlessly pairs an outside-in investigative lens with ground-up human testimony and internal insights. The film reflects on AJE’s historic coverage of global conflicts, the climate crisis, genocide and more in a drastically changing media landscape, all while balancing difficult decisions regarding where to focus resources, battling stigma as state-funded media and weathering the targeting of the channel’s journalists and bureaus while trying to remain true to AJE’s core principles.

articles.title: 15 de novembro: por que Proclamação da República é chamada de 'golpe'? | G1
articles.standfirst: Quase um século e meio depois, tema ainda suscita debates sobre a Proclamação da República. Primeiras críticas apareceram meses após Marechal Deodoro da Fonseca proclamá-la.
articles.summary: Quase um século e meio depois, tema ainda suscita debates sobre a Proclamação da República. Primeiras críticas apareceram meses após Marechal Deodoro da Fonseca proclamá-la.
articles.body:
O quadro 'Proclamação da República', de Benedito Calixto, retrata a proclamação na imaginação do pintor. — Foto: Centro Cultural São Paulo via BBC

Meses após o Marechal Deodoro da Fonseca enganar a própria mulher, burlar as recomendações médicas e levantar da cama — onde havia passado a madrugada daquele 15 de novembro febril — para proclamar a República brasileira, o país já conhecia a primeira crítica articulada sobre o processo que havia removido a monarquia do poder em 1889.

Escrito pelo advogado paulistano Eduardo Prado, o livro Fastos da Ditadura Militar no Brasil, de 1890, argumentava que a Proclamação da República no Brasil — celebrada como feriado no dia 15 de novembro — tinha sido uma cópia do modelo dos Estados Unidos aplicada a um contexto social e a um povo com características distintas.

A monarquia, segundo ele, ainda era o modelo mais adequado para a sociedade que se tinha no país. Prado também foi o primeiro autor a considerar a Proclamação da República um "golpe de Estado ilegítimo" aplicado pelos militares.

Hoje, quase um século e meio depois, o tema ainda suscita debates: enquanto diversos historiadores apontam a importância da chegada da República ao Brasil , apesar de suas incoerências e dificuldades, um movimento que ganhou força nos últimos anos — principalmente nas redes sociais — ainda a contesta.

"A proclamação foi um golpe de uma minoria escravocrata aliada aos grandes latifundiários, aos militares, a segmentos da Igreja e da maçonaria. O que é fato notório é que foi um golpe ilegítimo", disse à BBC News Brasil o empresário Luiz Philippe de Orleans e Bragança, tataraneto de D. Pedro 2º, o último imperador brasileiro, e militante do movimento de direita Acorda Brasil.

Em 2018, ele recebeu 118.457 votos no Estado de São Paulo e se elegeu deputado federal pelo PSL , então partido de Jair Bolsonaro, também eleito presidente naquele ano.

Retrato do Marechal Deodoro da Fonseca por Henrique Bernardelli; ele proclamou a República no Brasil. — Foto: Museu Histórico Nacional via BBC

"Quando há ilegitimidade na proclamação de qualquer modelo de governo, não se consegue estabelecer autoridade e, dessa forma, não se tem ordem. É exatamente isso que aconteceu na República: removeram o monarca e, no momento seguinte, foi um caos", acrescentou Orleans e Bragança, justificando a partir da história os solavancos recentes da democracia brasileira.

O processo de impeachment da presidente Dilma Rousseff ( PT ), em 2016, deu novo gás ao movimento pró-monarquia, impulsionado pela internet e pela presença de grupos monarquistas nas manifestações contra o governo petista, entre 2015 e 2016 — muitos deles, empunhando bandeiras do Brasil Império.

A ideia de que a Proclamação da República foi um "golpe" é reforçada pelo historiador José Murilo de Carvalho, que escreveu um livro sobre os períodos monárquico e republicano do Brasil, O Pecado Original da República.

Um dos intelectuais mais respeitados no país, Murilo também admite que é possível discutir a legitimidade do processo, como reivindicam os monarquistas atuais.

"Para se sustentar [a reivindicação de legitimidade da proclamação], ela teria que supor que a minoria republicana, predominantemente composta de bacharéis, jornalistas, advogados, médicos, engenheiros, alunos das escolas superiores, além dos cafeicultores paulistas, representava os interesses da maioria esmagadora da população ou do país todo. Um tanto complicado", avalia.

Ainda segundo Murilo, não apenas foi um golpe, como ele não contou com a participação popular, o que fortalece o argumento de ilegitimidade apresentado pelos atuais monarquistas. Para ele, a distância da maior camada da população das decisões políticas é um problema que perdura até hoje.

"Embora os propagandistas falassem em democracia, o pecado foi a ausência de povo, não só na proclamação, mas pelo menos até o fim da Primeira República. Incorporar plenamente o povo no sistema político é ainda hoje um problema da nossa República. Pode-se dizer que as condições do país não permitiram outra solução e que os propagandistas eram sonhadores. Muitos realmente eram", conta.

Após quase um século e meio, Proclamação da República ainda é alvo de debates. — Foto: Reuters via BBC

Monarquia como opção de regime político?

Especialista no período, o jornalista e historiador Laurentino Gomes, autor da trilogia 1808, 1822 e 1889, concorda com a leitura do "golpe". Para ele, no entanto, o debate sobre a legitimidade da República é sobre "quem legitima o quê", o que está ligado ao processo de consolidação de qualquer regime político.

"O termo 'legitimidade' é muito relativo. Depende do que se considera o instrumento legitimador da nossa República. Se ele for o voto, ela não é legítima, porque o Partido Republicano nunca teve apoio nas urnas. Agora, se considerar esse instrumento a força das armas, foi um movimento legítimo, porque foi por meio delas que o Exército consolidou o regime", diz.

Para Laurentino, a questão envolve a luta pelo direito de nomear os acontecimentos históricos que, no caso dos republicanos, conseguiram emplacar a ideia de "proclamação" e não de "golpe".

"O que aconteceu em 1889, em 1930 e em 1964 é a mesma coisa: Exército na rua fazendo política. Depende de quem legitima o quê. O movimento de 1964 não foi legitimado pela sociedade, mas a revolução de 1930 o foi tanto pelos sindicatos quanto pelas mudanças promovidas por Getúlio Vargas. A proclamação é contada hoje por quem venceu", argumenta.

Para o historiador Marcos Napolitano, professor da Faculdade de Filosofia, Letras e Ciências Humanas (FFLCH) da Universidade de São Paulo (USP), é possível, sim, falar em golpe na fundação da República. Já questionar sua legitimidade, como faz Orleans e Bragança, seria um revisionismo histórico que ele considera incabível.

"Se pensarmos que a monarquia era um regime historicamente vinculado à escravidão (esta sim, uma instituição ilegítima, sob quaisquer aspectos), acho pessoalmente que a fundação da República foi um processo político legítimo que, infelizmente, não veio acompanhado de reformas democratizantes e inclusivas", explica.

Segundo José Murilo de Carvalho, é possível afirmar que a proclamação foi obra quase totalmente dos militares, assim como conta o jornalista Laurentino Gomes em seu livro 1889 .

"Só poucos dias antes do golpe é que líderes civis foram envolvidos", explica Murilo. Para o professor Marcos Napolitano, porém, o fato de ter sido uma minoria a responsável por derrubar a monarquia não retira do movimento a sua legitimidade.

"Qualquer processo político está ligado à capacidade de minorias ativas ganharem o apoio de maiorias, ativas ou passivas, e neutralizarem outros grupos que lhes são contra. Nem sempre um processo político que começa com uma minoria ativa redunda em falta de democracia", explica Napolitano.

"Esta é a medida de legitimidade de um processo político. Muitos processos políticos democratizantes, que mudaram a história mundial, começaram assim. O que não os exime de serem processos muitas vezes traumáticos e conflitivos", ele acrescenta.

Orleans e Bragança expressa uma alternativa que já existe há algum tempo entre um grupo restrito de historiadores. O mais militante deles é o professor Armando Alexandre dos Santos, da Universidade do Sul de Santa Catarina (Unisul).

Frequentemente convidado pela Casa Real para palestras e eventos, ele é amigo pessoal de D. Luiz Gastão de Orleans e Bragança — que seria o imperador do país caso o Brasil fosse uma monarquia — desde os anos 1980.

Para Santos, a República representou a instauração de uma ditadura jamais vivida até então no Brasil.

"Foi uma quartelada de uma minoria revoltosa de militares que não teve nenhum apoio popular. A própria proclamação foi um show de indecisões: Deodoro da Fonseca, por exemplo, só decidiu proclamá-la porque foi pressionado pelos membros do seu grupinho que precisavam de um militar de patente para representá-los. Foi, acima de tudo, um modismo, uma imitação servil dos EUA", argumenta.

Santos, no entanto, não encontra apoio para sua tese na maior parte da academia. Para os historiadores ouvidos pela BBC News Brasil, o retorno à monarquia não está no horizonte político do país.

"O plebiscito de 1993 (para determinar a forma de governo do país) mostrou que há sólida maioria favorável à República, apesar das trapalhadas do regime. Fora do Carnaval, a imagem predominante da monarquia ainda é a de regime retrógrado", afirma José Murilo de Carvalho, seguido por Gomes.

"Em um momento de discussão da identidade nacional, se somos violentos ou pacíficos, corruptos ou transparentes, vamos em busca de mitos fundadores. Um deles é D. Pedro, que era um homem culto e respeitado. Esse movimento monárquico atual é freudiano. É a busca de pai que resolva tudo sem que a gente se preocupe", finaliza.

articles.title: Trump culpa governo Biden por paralisação nacional de voos nos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Declaração ocorreu após pane nas comunicações suspender decolagens por cerca de quatro horas e causar milhares de cancelamentos e atrasos.
articles.summary: Declaração ocorreu após pane nas comunicações suspender decolagens por cerca de quatro horas e causar milhares de cancelamentos e atrasos.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , culpou neste domingo (15) o governo de seu antecessor, Joe Biden , pela paralisação dos voos em todo o país na sexta-feira, que provocou cancelamentos e atrasos em viagens domésticas e internacionais .

Em seus primeiros comentários sobre a paralisação, Trump classificou como “um desastre” a gestão da aviação durante o governo do democrata Joe Biden . Na sexta-feira, autoridades americanas suspenderam as decolagens em todo o país por mais de quatro horas após uma falha durante trabalhos de atualização do sistema.

"Tudo em que eles tocaram deu errado", escreveu o presidente republicano na plataforma Truth Social.

"Muito dinheiro gasto de forma imprudente, deixando um sistema velho e quebrado ainda pior do que era quando começaram", acrescentou.

Biden, que governou de 2021 a 2025, sucedeu Trump após o primeiro mandato do republicano, de 2017 a 2021, e o antecedeu no atual mandato.

A FAA suspendeu todas as decolagens no país por cerca de quatro horas na sexta-feira (13), após uma falha nos sistemas de comunicação dos centros de controle de tráfego aéreo. A medida provocou milhares de cancelamentos e atrasos nos Estados Unidos e também afetou voos internacionais.

Segundo o governo americano, o problema ocorreu durante um serviço de manutenção para a substituição de cabos de cobre por fibra óptica em uma rede operada pela L3Harris, empresa contratada pela FAA. Um roteador teria apresentado problemas e provocado instabilidade em outros equipamentos da rede.

As autoridades ainda investigam se a falha foi causada por erro humano ou por um equipamento defeituoso. O governo afirmou não acreditar que tenha ocorrido um ataque cibernético e descartou uma relação com o novo sistema de inteligência artificial usado pela FAA.

A paralisação foi a segunda medida nacional desse tipo desde os ataques de 11 de setembro de 2001. A anterior ocorreu em janeiro de 2023, durante o governo de Joe Biden , depois de uma falha no sistema de informações aeronáuticas da FAA.

articles.body:
A diarista Irismar Vieira Damasceno, de 55 anos, faz o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio pela primeira vez, após ser incentivada por uma das filhas e professores. Depois da tensão do primeiro dia devido ao medo de zerar a prova ou ser desclassificada, ela está confiante neste domingo (15) e espera conseguir nota suficiente para cursar uma faculdade.

"Antes eu não tinha expectativas, eu achava que eu não me encaixava em nada além do trabalho que eu já exercia desde adolescente, que é doméstica e de serviços gerais. Eu sempre olhava para as outras profissões e achava que eu não daria conta, que não era capaz. Hoje eu acho que eu consigo fazer alguma coisa", contou ao g1 .

Natural do Piauí, ela mora em Goiás há 10 anos. Em 2023, ela voltou a estudar. "Eu não tinha terminado nem o ensino fundamental. Esse ano eu concluo o ensino médico", contou. Irismar ainda não decidiu qual carreira quer seguir, mas pensa na área da Saúde ou direito.

Irismar Vieira Damasceno faz o Enem em Goiânia, Goiás — Foto: Yanca Cristina/g1 Goiás

Quem também faz o Enem neste domingo é a babá Maria Gabriela Dias, 31 anos. Ela conta que voltou ao Brasil e quer cursar direito em uma faculdade pública.

"Tentei há um tempo fazer direito, fui embora do país, voltei e agora quero tentar de novo. A expectativa é mudar de vida", afirmou.

Maria Gabriela Dias, 31 anos, faz o Enem em Goiânia, Goiás — Foto: Yanca Cristina/g1 Goiás

Irismar e Maria Gabriela estão entre os mais de 160 mil candidatos que se inscreveram para o Enem em Goiás. No estado, mais de 100 mil são mulheres e 66,2 mil são homens.

Neste segundo dia de Enem, a prova é composta por 90 questões objetivas, sendo 45 de matemática e suas tecnologia e 45 de ciências da natureza e suas tecnologias.

Assim como no primeiro dia de provas, os portões foram abertos às 12h e fechados às 13h, com o exame começando às 13h30. Os estudantes só podem deixar o local após duas horas da aplicação das provas.

articles.title: Swiss men take to streets, call for stronger fight against violence against women
articles.summary: Hundreds of men gathered outside parliament in the Swiss capital on Saturday to protest against misogyny and violence against women, calling on men to
articles.body: Hundreds of men gathered outside parliament in the Swiss capital on Saturday to protest against misogyny and violence against women, calling on men to take a more active and vocal role in challenging both.The demonstration, titled “Men against Violence against Women”, came amid growing concerns over the spread of misogynistic views among teenage boys and young men, particularly online. Organisers and campaigners have called for men to build a stronger counter-narrative to such attitudes.The rally also followed increased visibility for influencers associated with the right-wing “manosphere”, some of whom were emboldened by US President Donald Trump's 2024 election victory to amplify misogynistic insults and threats online, according to news agency the Associated Press (AP).Study highlights concerns over attitudes towards masculinitySwiss academics and advocacy groups have, for the first time, attempted to assess the scale of the manosphere movement in the country.A survey published in June by the University of Zurich and mencare, an umbrella organisation representing Swiss men's and fathers' groups, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 expressed concern that “real men are increasingly marginalized in society”.The study also found that half of those surveyed held a restrictive, dominance-based view of masculinity.It called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, adding that the discussion should begin in schools.The Swiss government has also taken up the issue. Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month aimed at raising awareness about the dangers of violent online abuse directed at women.In a speech on November 2, Jans cited figures showing that men committed four-fifths of violent crimes. The proportion was even higher in rape cases, where men accounted for 99% of perpetrators, he said.“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”Organisers call on men to challenge misogynyThe demonstration sought to encourage young men influenced by the manosphere, as well as those exposed to patriarchal attitudes more broadly, to reconsider their views and challenge violence against women and queer people.Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker and co-organiser of the rally alongside the group Maenner, said men needed to acknowledge their role in the problem and take responsibility for addressing it.“We men are part of the problem — the problem being violence against women and queer people,” Gosteli said.“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say: We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution,” he added.The rally's central message was that men should not remain silent on misogyny and violence, but take a more visible role in opposing them.You use AI every day. articles.body: CHENNAI: The Tamil Nadu government has suspended five library officials over the procurement of AI-generated books for the Periyar Arivulagam Library in Coimbatore.According to an announcement made by school education minister A Rajmohan on Sunday, those suspended are S Kamatchi, chief librarian, Anna Centenary Library (ACL), Chennai; Dinesh Kumar, chief librarian and information officer (in-charge), Kalaignar Centenary Library, Madurai; V Santhanakrishnan, librarian and information officer, Kalaignar Centenary Library, Madurai, and in-charge of the Periyar Arivulagam Library; S Santhana Karthikeyan, librarian and information officer, ACL, Chennai; and J Juliet, chief accounts officer, Directorate of Public Libraries.The minister said the irregularities had occurred during the previous DMK regime.The alleged irregularities came to light after writer Perumal Murugan identified nearly 1,800 books from Agal Vilakku Pathippagam in the library’s fourth-floor Tamil section.The books reportedly carried inflated prices, AI-generated misinformation, fictitious author names and invalid International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).Writers and researchers subsequently flagged similar irregularities elsewhere.Researchers have also raised concerns about the library’s English-language books. articles.title: IndiGo flight’s landing gear fails to retract after take-off, makes safe emergency landing in Pune
articles.summary: PUNE: A full emergency was declared at the Pune airport on Sunday morning after a Guwahati bound IndiGo flight (6E 0623) with 192 persons on board,
articles.body: PUNE: A full emergency was declared at the Pune airport on Sunday morning after a Guwahati bound IndiGo flight (6E 0623) with 192 persons on board, including passengers and crew, reported a technical issue shortly after take-off.The pilot informed Air Traffic Control (ATC) that the aircraft’s landing gear (undercarriage) had failed to retract after take-off and remained in the extended position. Airport officials said that immediately upon receiving the information, they coordinated with ATC, IndiGo and all concerned agencies."The Indian Air Force (IAF) declared a Full Emergency, following which all prescribed emergency response procedures were promptly activated. Fire services, ambulance services and other emergency response teams were placed on high alert to ensure the safety of passengers and crew," Pune airport director Santosh Dhoke said.As a precautionary measure, the aircraft conducted a low pass over the runway to facilitate a visual assessment of the landing gear. Subsequently, the aircraft landed safely at Pune Airport at around 9am."Following the landing, the aircraft was escorted to Bay number- 7 by three fire-fighting vehicles and two ambulances, in accordance with the prescribed emergency response procedures. After confirmation of the aircraft’s safe and normal status, ATC declared the full emergency withdrawn at 9.10am. Thereafter, the aerobridge was connected, and all passengers were safely deboarded," the director added.All 192 persons on board, including passengers and crew, were safe, and no injuries were reported. articles.title: ‘For sure not in 2027’: Nato scraps leaders’ summit in Albania amid defence spending Ukraine war concerns
articles.summary: Nato will not hold a leaders' summit in Albania next year, with the alliance scaling back high-level meetings amid tensions over defence spending, Iran
articles.body: Nato will not hold a leaders' summit in Albania next year, with the alliance scaling back high-level meetings amid tensions over defence spending, Iran and the war in Ukraine.However, Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte played down the decision, saying the alliance was flexible about when to hold such gatherings, AP reported on Monday.On Thursday, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said that there was no common position on when the summit would take place, but ruled out 2027. He said Tirana could host the event in 2028 if a summit is held that year.“There is not yet a common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027,” Rama said. “In 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana.”Rutte said the meeting would be held as necessary.“We are flexible with Nato summits,” Rutte told The Associated Press in an interview. “We have summits when we need them,” he said, adding that the next one would be held “when a necessity is there”.Nato previously held summits every two years, until about a decade ago.Ministerial meetings also being scaled backThe reduction in high-level gatherings extends beyond meetings between US President Donald Trump and other Nato leaders.Nato defence ministers usually meet in October, but no meeting was held last month, and none is planned for October 2027. Foreign ministers are scheduled to meet only once next year, instead of twice, under what thealliance describes as a “reorganisation package”.US defence secretary Pete Hegseth and secretary of state Marco Rubio have each skipped a NATO meeting or left before talks concluded since taking office. Hegseth has used defence ministerial gatherings to criticise or pressure European allies and Canada, AP reported.Albania's defence spending raises questionsAlbania was named as the host for next year's summit in 2025, but its name was removed from a declaration issued after a NATO meeting in July.Some allies believe Albania is not spending enough on defence and were reluctant to reward it with the alliance's major event. The government in Tirana is projected to spend 2.15 per cent of its gross domestic product on defence this year.Nato's target is for its 32 members to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035, with a further 1.5 per cent allocated to defence-related infrastructure. Albania is not the worst performer among member states, with Spain, Belgium and Slovenia spending considerably less.Hosting a summit carries financial and political costsOrganising a Nato summit requires substantial resources and can carry political costs for the host country.The Netherlands reportedly spent a year preparing for the 2025 summit in The Hague, with an investment of around $100 million. Officials said Nato would have needed to make a decision on Albania by October to give the country enough time to organise next year's event.Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted this year's summit gala at his palace complex in Ankara. According to AP, Turkey refurbished a military airport for the arrival of leaders and deployed tens of thousands of security personnel, effectively shutting down parts of the capital. articles.title: Bengaluru man buys liquor worth Rs 2,170, objects to paying Rs 20 for carry bag bearing store's own name and logo; consumer commission calls it unfair trade practice and deficiency in service, orders Tonique to refund Rs 20 and pay Rs 5,000 compensation and Rs 3,000 litigation costs
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The bag was meant only to carry the booze home, but it ended up killing the buzz for a liquor store.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The bag was meant only to carry the booze home, but it ended up killing the buzz for a liquor store. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Bangalore (Urban), held a liquor store guilty of unfair trade practice and deficiency in service for charging a Bagalagunte resident Rs 20 for a carry bag stamped with its own name and logo.It all started on June 3, 2025, when Theerthesh BS, 33, bought beverages worth Rs 2,170 from Tonique, a liquor store on Kasturba Road. Since the bottles were fragile, he asked for a carry bag. The store gave him one bearing its brand name, logo and other promotional content, and raised a separate bill of Rs 20 for it on the same day and at the same time.Theerthesh said he objected to paying for a bag that carried the store’s own logo and identification details, but the store’s staff rejected his request. With no other way to carry the bottles safely, he paid. He then filed a complaint on June 17, seeking a refund of Rs 20, compensation of Rs 25,000 for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, and other relief.Despite notice from the commission, Tonique, represented by its manager, neither appeared nor filed its version, and was placed ex parte. Later, Tonique’s counsel did file written arguments. The store said when a customer asks for a carry bag, they are told about the charges, which are displayed on a board in all its outlets, and a bill is raised. The store thus admitted that it sells carry bags on request after a purchase.The commission, comprising president Ramachandra MS and members Nandini H Kumbhar and Savitha Airani, invoking the principle of “Caveat Venditor”, meaning “let the seller be aware”, said a seller of beverage bottles should know every customer will need a bag to carry such products.Charging customers for a bag used for its own advertising also amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, it held.The commission further noted that Tonique’s failure to appear was a clear admission of the allegations. articles.title: Pakistani handler used romantic relationship to recruit woman for Rajasthan Railway track blast: Probe
articles.summary: JAISALMER: The conspiracy behind the November 3 blast on a railway track near 50 GB village in Rajasthan's Sri Ganganagar district was allegedly
articles.body: JAISALMER: The conspiracy behind the November 3 blast on a railway track near 50 GB village in Rajasthan's Sri Ganganagar district was allegedly masterminded by a Pakistan-based ISI handler identified as Shah, who used a romantic relationship to recruit a young woman to carry out the attack.The accused were allegedly paid Rs 2.23 lakh for executing the operation, including Rs 1 lakh in cash, while the remaining amount was transferred to their bank accounts.The primary objective behind the railway track blast, allegedly orchestrated by the ISI, was to spread terror across Rajasthan, particularly in Sri Ganganagar.ADGP ATS Dinesh MN, along with senior officials of AGTF, ANTF, Bikaner Range IG Om Prakash and Sri Ganganagar SP Harishankar, disclosed details of the investigation at a press conference on Sunday.The Rajasthan Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) and Sri Ganganagar police, with assistance from Punjab Counter Intelligence, arrested two accused, including 21-year-old Mahakdeep Kaur and Davinder Singh (23), from Gurdaspur in Punjab.Police recovered two foreign-made pistols, 46 live cartridges and Rs 30,000 in cash from the arrested accused.Also check: Blast damages Rajasthan railway track near Pakistan borderDinesh MN said the blast was carried out at the direction of a foreign-based handler whose objective was to spread panic in Sri Ganganagar and across Rajasthan. The handler allegedly provided the target location, funding and instructions for executing the attack.Investigations revealed that Mahakdeep Kaur had married around two years ago, but her marriage ended in December 2024. In February 2025, her husband, Karanveer Singh, was jailed in an NDPS case. Subsequently, he re-established contact with her and allegedly asked her to communicate with a Pakistan-based person named Lovely, who would provide money to be delivered to him in jail.Lovely later introduced her to another person identified as Shah. Gradually, conversations between Mahakdeep and Shah developed into a romantic relationship, and she became emotionally attached to him. The Pakistani handler allegedly exploited this relationship to recruit her for the railway blast and assign her targets.According to the ADGP, Mahakdeep and Davinder visited the Ramsinghpur area on October 6, but their first attempt failed because explosives were not available. They returned on October 12 or 13 with explosives and a timer, but a technical malfunction prevented the blast. Following further instructions from Pakistan, they allegedly succeeded in triggering the explosion near 50 GB on November 3. Investigators are also examining whether a train was the intended target.The breakthrough came after an extensive investigation involving the analysis of nearly five lakh call records and the questioning of more than 400 people. Police also examined suspected Pakistan-linked smugglers and their local contacts before tracing the accused through technical surveillance and human intelligence.Dinesh MN said inputs from central agencies received three days ago led ATS teams to Punjab. articles.title: Iran says it targets US radar in Bahrain. What do we know?
articles.summary: Bahrain Defence Force says its air defence systems thwart several Iranian ‘aerial attacks’.
articles.body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what it describes as hostile US actions.

Sirens sounded in Bahrain on Sunday as its Ministry of Interior urged residents to “remain calm” and “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It was the second time in three days that the IRGC claimed to have targeted a US radar system in Bahrain.

The US military said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday but has yet to comment on Sunday’s claim.

The IRGC said it struck the radar at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, according to a statement carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency.

Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts within about three hours, the first about 4:30am (01:30 GMT). The ministry warned of a “potential threat” and urged residents to seek shelter. It gave no further details about the threat.

The Bahrain Defence Force also said its air defence systems thwarted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom.

In its statement, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and claimed that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway had failed. It warned that any US attack would draw a more severe response.

The IRGC said on Friday that it destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, saying it had shot down two IRGC drones and there were no injuries or damage.

In a statement carried by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency, the IRGC called the operation a “serious warning” over what it described as aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Friday marked the first time since early September that Iran had claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.

Tehran has told the United Nations Security Council it would respond immediately to renewed US or Israeli attacks and has accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of supporting US military operations. Bahrain has called for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region and demanded they stop.

Manama, Bahrain, is where the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet is based. A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks had damaged or destroyed buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.

What has happened in the Strait of Hormuz?

The IRGC’s navy said two oil tankers struck sea mines on Saturday while trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state news agency IRNA, it said the vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems and were using what it called an “unauthorised” route.

The IRGC said two other tankers turned back towards the Gulf after receiving warnings from its maritime traffic control centre.

Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Mohammed Vall said on Saturday that there were “two similar incidents yesterday” and the number of tankers hitting mines has increased.

Vall said Iran claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under its “full control” and “only Iran and Oman have the right to control it”. The United States rejects that claim.

According to Vall, Iran blamed the incidents on the tanker owners and the countries backing them, saying they had failed to comply with the regulations Iran imposed on passage through the strait.

Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled with Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, telling Al Jazeera that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.

Ghalibaf said in the interview last week that Iran has conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

US President Donald Trump’s administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.

Saeid Golkar, the UC Foundation associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, told Al Jazeera that limited exchanges could escalate into a wider war.

“Both sides may prefer to avoid a full-scale war, but the danger lies in miscalculation,” Golkar said.

“Iran may continue limited maritime and regional escalation to increase pressure while Washington could respond militarily. Such exchanges could eventually lead to a broader conflict that neither side initially intended.”

articles.title: Drone attacks on power stations plunge Sudan’s cities into darkness
articles.summary: Sudan’s power stations are being targeted in waves of drone attacks, resulting in power outages.
articles.body:
Port Sudan, Sudan – Kamal Mohammed, 42, has spent years managing his diabetes. But prolonged power cuts in the al-Taqaddum neighbourhood of Port Sudan, where he lives, have made his life “catastrophic”, he says.

Kamal relies on regular insulin injections to manage his diabetes, but unstable electricity supplies make it difficult for him to keep track of the doses he needs or store the medication at the required temperature.

“I need an insulin dose every day, but sometimes I have to skip it when power cuts last so long that the refrigerator loses its cooling,” he said.

Kamal’s story reflects the massive disruptions the war between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), which broke out in April 2023, has wrought on civilians across Sudan.

More than 14 million civilians have been displaced since 2023, including about 4.5 million to neighbouring countries, while more than 150,000 people are believed to have been killed.

The fighting between the SAF and RSF, two former military allies, has increasingly turned into a conflict in which civilians and civilian infrastructure are targets. Drone attacks killed more than 160 people in just a few days in western Sudan in October, while hospitals, displacement camps and markets have become targets.

Attacks on energy infrastructure have also severely affected healthcare infrastructure, aid groups and other services vital for civilian life.

The RSF has intensified attacks on power stations around Khartoum state over the past month, creating an energy crisis in the capital. There has been no clear schedule for the power cuts in Khartoum caused by the damage to energy infrastructure, but blackouts can last anywhere between six hours and a day.

Between October 20 and November 2, 2026, there were at least 18 attacks on electricity infrastructure across at least nine states, leading to declining power generation capacity and fuel shortages.

Repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100MW today, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Mohammed al-Husseini, a political analyst, noted that the RSF stepped up attacks on civilian infrastructure after the SAF captured strategically important towns in the Kordofan region and other areas in recent weeks.

“The attacks on power stations aimed to weaken Sudan’s economy and disrupt agricultural and industrial production, both heavily dependent on a reliable electricity supply, particularly as the country prepares for a new agricultural season,” al-Husseini said.

“The attacks also sought to disrupt essential services and deepen humanitarian pressures, given electricity’s role in supplying water, maintaining communications and keeping medical facilities, including dialysis centres, operational.”

The United Nations has warned about the harrowing effect these attacks are having on civilians already plunged into abject poverty due to the war.

“I don’t know where those drone strikes are originating from; we need help passing the message to whoever needs to hear it, that this must stop,” Denise Brown, UN resident and humanitarian coordinator, recently said.

“There is no defence for repeatedly hitting power stations and fuel stations. People who need lifesaving dialysis can’t get it. Women are giving birth with no lights in the hospital. Operations can’t take place.”

With refrigeration no longer a viable option for storing insulin, some people are now buying ice to keep their medicine cool, but not everyone can afford this daily expense.

“I can barely afford my medication as my salary is not more than 150,000 Sudanese pounds [$14.4]. Buying even a small block of ice could cost me 7,000 pounds [$0.67] a day,” Kamal said.

Electricity supplies were far more stable before fighting began, he said. During the summer, power cuts were limited and rarely lasted more than four hours. Now they are frequent, and the pressure this has caused on the national grid has made utilities even more expensive for customers.

“Before the war, my monthly electricity bill was no more than 3,000 pounds [$0.28]. Now it can reach 100,000 pounds [$9.61], although sometimes it is lower because of the prolonged cuts,” said Kamal.

Those who can afford them have bought solar panels for a more reliable supply, but these systems cost between 4 and 6 million pounds ($385 to $577), putting them out of reach of most households in Port Sudan.

“I considered getting a solar power system to keep my insulin refrigerated, run fans for my children and charge our phones at home. But it is far beyond what I can afford,” Kamal said. “Every day, I have to look for somewhere with a generator where I can charge my phone.”

The energy crisis has left businesses struggling to operate. Osama Omar, 22, is an engineering student who opened a laundry in the Deim Madina neighbourhood of Port Sudan about six months ago to cover his basic living expenses. But prolonged power cuts threaten his small laundry business, which relies heavily on electricity.

“For nearly a month now, the supply has become increasingly unreliable, with outages lasting more than 24 hours,” Omar told Al Jazeera.

He has tried to adapt his business to the rolling power outages, but their unpredictability makes this difficult, leaving laundry piling up at his premises. At times, he has had to turn down new orders.

“Running my business in Sudan already comes with many challenges because of the war, the unstable exchange rate and rising operating costs,” Omar told Al Jazeera. “But power cuts have become another war that Sudanese people are being forced to fight.”

The energy crisis is felt across the country, with camps hosting Sudan’s millions of displaced people being particularly hard hit.

Sabri Adam, deputy head of the committee overseeing al-Karama 3 displacement camp in al-Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile state, told Al Jazeera that the 3,000 residents there are struggling to cope with the situation.

“Many arrived with little more than the clothes they were wearing, leaving behind their homes and belongings,” he told Al Jazeera. “The camp has no electricity supply, relying on just three large floodlights for lighting – one near the communal toilets and two beside the water tanks.”

Those with chronic illnesses such as diabetes, who need to store their medication at certain temperatures, have been badly affected.

Azhar Abdullah, a displaced woman living in al-Karama 3, said the lack of access to water and electricity has worsened the situation for her 13-year-old daughter, who has a thyroid disorder that requires extra care.

“Her heart rate increases and she experiences severe pain when she has to wash clothes by hand or exert herself physically,” Abdullah told Al Jazeera. “I worry that her condition will deteriorate further, as she has to undertake strenuous tasks throughout the day amid the lack of basic services.”

images.caption: Workers assess damage at the al-Markhiyat power station north of Omdurman, Sudan, on October 28, 2026, following a drone attack [Ebrahim Hamid/AFP]
Kamal Mohammed, who has diabetes, struggles to keep his insulin at the required temperature amid unreliable electricity supplies [Fatima Edam/Al Jazeera]
Unpredictable power cuts have disrupted Osama Omar’s laundry business in Port Sudan, leaving orders unfinished and piles of clothes waiting to be washed [Fatima Edam/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections. The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press. Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said. The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They are also expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts. “We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says. The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.” Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds. “That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay. Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.” But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China. ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea. Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials. Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping. “The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said. He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia. “In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.” China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.

images.caption: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. hands the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DECA) to ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn, while Philippine Secretary of Trade and Industry Maria Cristina Roque looks on .

articles.title: Philippines, Australia sign defense pact with eye on China
articles.summary: MANILA — The Philippines and Australia signed a defense cooperation arrangement on Sunday that Manila said ​would lower bureaucratic hurdles to joint military activities, as the two countries ‌further deepen security ties.
articles.body: MANILA — The Philippines and Australia signed a defense cooperation arrangement on Sunday that Manila said ​would lower bureaucratic hurdles to joint military activities, as the two countries ‌further deepen security ties. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the arrangement would streamline implementation of the bilateral Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, or SOVFA, by simplifying coordination procedures. “Rather than 100 steps to do ​a single thing, it will just now take 10,” Teodoro told reporters, ​describing the deal as an “anti-red tape measure” for implementing SOVFA. He said the ⁠arrangement would pave the way for closer cooperation involving maritime, air and land ​forces, as well as humanitarian and disaster response, and would bolster the Philippines’ “credible deterrence posture”, ​including in the South China Sea. China’s defense and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent on Sunday. The Philippines has been broadening its network of security ties while complementing a ​long-standing alliance with its treaty partner, the United States, in the face of ​what it describes as China’s aggressive behaviour in the South China Sea, where countries have overlapping maritime ‌claims. Australia ⁠has consistently supported Manila’s position on the strategic waterway, backing a 2016 ruling by an international arbitral tribunal that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects. Beijing maintains that its actions in the South China Sea have been ​lawful and professional. ​It routinely opposes Manila’s ⁠joint military activities with its allied partners, saying such drills heighten tensions in the region. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese witnessed the ​signing of the defense pact in Manila, where he is attending ​a summit ⁠of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. He said the agreement would enhance maritime awareness and information sharing and increase strategic dialogue, training, interoperability and defense infrastructure development. Albanese announced additional ⁠Australian investment ​in maritime domain awareness, including drone technology, equipment ​and training aimed at improving detection of maritime and cybersecurity threats.

articles.title: Spain’s Canary Islands record highest daily migrant arrivals since 2020; 1,488 rescued
articles.summary: Spain's Canary Islands face unprecedented migrant arrivals, with 1,488 people rescued from boats, highlighting the growing crisis on the Atlantic migration route from West Africa.
articles.body: Spain’s Canary Islands recorded their highest number of migrant arrivals in a single day since 2020 after 1,488 people were rescued from 14 boats on Saturday, as the Atlantic migration route from West Africa saw a fresh increase in crossings, EFE news agency reported, citing the maritime rescue service.The latest arrivals surpassed the previous daily record of 1,461 people rescued in waters near the archipelago on November 7, 2020, according to maritime rescue authorities.The increase follows a rise in arrivals from West African countries since October, placing additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some islands. Smaller and less densely populated islands have been particularly affected.El Hierro, one of the smallest islands in the archipelago, received 12 of the 14 boats on Saturday. The remaining two arrived in Gran Canaria and Tenerife.One of the boats carried 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children. Authorities said those rescued were taken to El Hierro, with most coming from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea-Conakry.Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is scheduled to visit El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the increase in migrant arrivals.The Atlantic crossing from West Africa to the Canary Islands remains one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Thousands of people attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, risking rough seas, strong currents and long distances in an effort to reach Spanish territory.Crossings typically increase during autumn, when sea conditions are generally calmer and more favourable for travel.Despite the latest surge, overall arrivals to the Canary Islands remain lower than last year. articles.title: Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
articles.summary: Ukraine’s NATO ambition has always been a red line for the Kremlin. Giving up territory has been a no-no for Ukraine.
articles.body:
The United States has pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia, almost five years into their war.

But the administration of President Donald Trump has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.

The idea, according to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was communicated to him by Trump’s negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week.

After the Abu Dhabi round of talks, Kushner and Witkoff met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday.

Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.

But the Kremlin has repeatedly said Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would demand “a harsh response” from Russia.

So will Washington’s latest pitch be acceptable to both Ukraine and Russia?

On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that Kushner and Witkoff had suggested that Ukraine could become a NATO member if it ceded control of Donbas in the east.

He said, “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'”

“NATO is back on the agenda” since it is part of an “extremely difficult” conversation between Ukraine and Russia which would determine the future of European security, Zelenskyy said.

Putin has been against Ukraine’s NATO membership and has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from countries bordering Russia.

“This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

“Real security in Europe means the EU [European Union] and NATO. That’s it. There is no other security in Europe.”

Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the US, told Al Jazeera that Washington’s proposal, if accurate, is significant because it articulates very directly an approach long current in US administration circles that Ukraine should be prepared to make territorial concessions in the service of a settlement.

“The NATO element seems very doubtful. Surely attractive to Ukraine, but [it is] hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to this. And some NATO members will be doubtful too,” he said.

Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, argued that the proposal was a major departure from previously held positions.

“The US has been very cautious about getting further involved in Ukraine, with the Biden administration giving military support, but clearly opposing any ideas of Western involvement on the ground. Trump has seemed to be very sympathetic to the Russian cause, and has had significant blow-ups with Zelenskyy, so this proposal is certainly a surprise,” he noted.

He told Al Jazeera that offering NATO membership in a peace settlement would give significant support to Ukraine should Russia reinitiate the conflict in the future.

“In the light of Trump’s repeated attacks on NATO, this could be seen as a recommitment to the alliance. However, there would be questions over whether Trump could bring other NATO allies to support the proposal,” he added.

What does the US proposal mean for Ukraine?

Ukraine applied to become a NATO member in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country.

Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.

But NATO members remain divided over offering Ukraine alliance membership amid an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.

NATO members bordering Russia, like Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join, amid concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.

But under President Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up on hopes of joining the alliance.

Yet, while the new proposal from Witkoff and Kushner revives Ukraine’s hopes of joining NATO, it demands a compromise that no government in Kyiv can easily make.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.

But he said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.

Featherstone noted that Ukraine has been fighting for a long time and has consistently maintained that it will not relinquish its territory in a peace deal.

“The proposal from the Trump administration is clearly an attempt to test this Ukrainian position, in an effort to confront the impasse,” he said.

“NATO membership would give a level of security that Ukraine would likely welcome. However, this would be a big sacrifice of territory and sovereignty. After years of Trump’s questioning of the NATO commitment, Ukraine would need a strong statement of commitment to its defence should they be considering any proposal like this,” he added.

What does the US proposal mean to Russia?

The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal.

But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.

Despite Kushner and Witkoff’s meetings with Putin, the Kremlin has shown little appetite for a change in that position. Moscow has continued, throughout the war, to demand that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions and maintain a neutral and demilitarised status. Russia has also firmly opposed any deployment of Western troops or peacekeepers on Ukrainian soil.

In addition to demanding that Ukraine give up its NATO dreams, Moscow has also insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.

Just as the new US proposal asks Ukraine to give up some territory in return for a NATO seat, it offers Russia a bargain — withdraw its red line on Ukraine’s NATO membership and get the Donbas in exchange.

The region in eastern Ukraine has historically been the country’s industrial heartland and is therefore a critical economic engine.

A majority of people in the Donbas identify as ethnically Ukrainian, but a minority identifies as ethnically Russian. The Russian language is also widely spoken in the region — a legacy of Russian migration there in the 19th century and then under the Soviet Union.

Russia accuses Ukraine of discriminating against Russian-speaking and ethnically Russian people in the Donbas and has used this claim to justify its demand that Kyiv hand over the region to Moscow.

The region consists of the provinces of Luhansk and Donetsk. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has occupied almost all of Luhansk and most of Donetsk. In all, it controls about 88 percent of the Donbas region. But it has consistently demanded that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the remaining parts of the Donbas they currently hold.

Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, told Al Jazeera the US proposal tests the extent to which the territory of Donbas really matters to Russia.

But he said the recent Abu Dhabi talks had shown that Russia wanted more than just territorial concessions from Ukraine.

“They [the Russians] want to discuss what they call a new European security architecture, which is a code name for Russia having veto [power] when it comes to NATO,” he said.

He noted that it was also interesting that the Americans did not put forward the idea of Kyiv ceding the Donbas to the Russians in exchange for NATO membership.

“But everything indicates that the Russians will never accept this,” he said, referring to the idea of Ukraine joining NATO.

“The Russians have no intention of actually coming to the negotiating table. They’re just bringing up new issues [currently about European security architecture] and broadening the agenda in order to make it look like they’re negotiating and appease the American leadership, while inflicting as much damage on Ukraine as possible,” he added.

The US has not explicitly announced that it has suggested Kyiv should cede territory for NATO membership.

On Saturday, hours after Zelenskyy’s remarks to reporters, in a lengthy post on X, Kushner suggested that “the press has reported some of the maximalist positions proposed by both sides, along with strong political rhetoric”.

He highlighted that the conversations between Russia, Ukraine and the US were “private discussions” aimed at ending the war.

“Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps,” he said.

“In our private discussions, both sides understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war. Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” he added.

Earlier, on Thursday, Kushner also told reporters that Putin has agreed to include Europe in peace negotiations.

“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” he said.
