articles.title: China stonewalls on cases of detained Americans, despite personal appeal from Trump
articles.summary: China has failed to engage with the U.S. over the fate of two Americans unjustly detained in the country, despite multiple personal appeals from President Trump and positive signals from Chinese President Xi Jinping. The lack of engagement on the Chinese side is out of character, according to sources close to the cases. The two…
articles.body:
China has failed to engage with the U.S. over the fate of two Americans unjustly detained in the country, despite multiple personal appeals from President Trump and positive signals from Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The lack of engagement on the Chinese side is out of character, according to sources close to the cases. The two Americans are Youlin Chen, a seismologist jailed for over two years, and Min Zin, an academic arrested in June.

Trump is likely to raise the cases again – a third time for Chen and a second time for Min Zin – when he meets Xi on the sidelines of the APEC summit, taking place in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19.

Min Zin was hospitalized in October, treated for dehydration, stomach illness and other ailments, adding urgency to his family’s push for his release.

“The beginning of December will mark 6 months of Min Zin’s detention. I continue to worry about the impacts of his imprisonment on both his physical and mental health,” Sylvia Zin, his wife, said in a statement to The Hill.

“I hope that President Trump will demand Min Zin’s immediate and unconditional release when he sees President Xi at the APEC Summit next week.”

Trump views freeing Americans and others unjustly jailed abroad as a pillar of his legacy, and the State Department says he has helped secure the release of at least 115 Americans.

The State Department has labeled both Min Zin and Chen as “wrongfully detained,” indicating that the Trump administration has looked into both their cases and determined any charges or allegations are unwarranted. Chen has been accused of espionage while Min Zin has not yet been charged.

Both cases are being handled by China’s Ministry of State Security. The MSS is China’s principal civilian intelligence service, responsible for conducting foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. It’s most comparable to the CIA, although it is reportedly much larger.

Advocates for Min Zin are hopeful there is a window to secure his release before charges are issued. Chinese authorities could say that they investigated suspicions but didn’t turn up anything, they argue. But they worry that if charges are imposed, it will set off a new timeline for a trial and sentencing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington D.C. rejected that the two Americans are wrongfully detained and said they are “suspected of engaging in activities that endanger China’s national security and violate Chinese law.”

“China is a law-based country. There is no such thing as so-called ‘wrongful detention’,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Chinese judicial authorities are handling the cases in accordance with law.”

In protest of China’s silence, the State Department in October elevated travel warnings for the country as posing a serious risk of wrongful detention of Americans, a so-called “D” risk indicator .

That “was a very clear signal from the Trump administration to the Chinese government that they have made commitments to resolve these cases and they have not taken action,” said Eric Lebson, who is helping advise the Chen family. Lebson is chief strategy officer for Global Reach, a nonprofit organization dedicated to bringing home Americans who are wrongly held abroad.

The U.S. believes China takes seriously the negative impact travel warnings have on a country’s image. Xi has talked about bringing 100,000 American students to the country over the next five years and is promoting China as a destination for international business.

“China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there,” Xi said in remarks at the White House during the State visit in September.

The travel warning for China remains at a Level Two, which means U.S. citizens should “exercise increased caution.” But the recent addition of the D indicator suggests the State Department is considering elevating the risk to a Level Three, in which people are advised to reconsider travel to the country.

“That’s significant because it will impact the ability of American businesses and universities and others to allow travel to China and that will have a serious reputational and economic impact on China,” Lebson said.

Of the seven countries the State Department has “D” indicators on, five are at a Level Three or Level Four – Do Not Travel. The list includes Afghanistan, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Nicaragua.

Congress is also trying to increase pressure on China to release Chen and Min Zin. House and Senate resolutions introduced in September suggested imposing a “D” indicator to increase pressure on Beijing — marking a rare moment of cooperation between bipartisan members of Congress and the Trump administration.

The bipartisan and bicameral resolutions came ahead of Trump hosting Xi for a State visit.

The resolution condemns China for jailing Chen and Min Zin, and advocates for raising the travel advisory to a Level Three. It further calls on the State Department to review whether China fits the category of a State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention.

The resolution text says that the practice has “harmed the prospects for scientific collaboration and people-to-people exchanges between the United States and the People’s Republic of China.”

Trump created the label in September 2025 by executive order, and it was codified by Congress later that year. The Trump administration has so far applied it to Afghanistan and Iran.

China protested the U.S. creating the label, and rejected that Beijing engages in unjust jailings.

“There is no so-called issue of ‘wrongful detention’ in China,” Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian said at the time.

“It is well known that wrongful detention, arbitrary detention, coercive diplomacy, long-arm jurisdiction and unilateral sanctions are among the U.S.’s favorite tools.”

articles.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over church mass shooting
articles.summary: The attack on funeral at a Greek Orthodox church killed nine and injured 34 others last month.
articles.body:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.

The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".

The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.

A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.

It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.

Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.

"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."

The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.

They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them , the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.

King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".

The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.

Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.

Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.

Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

articles.title: 'Purge'-masked suspect accused of killing college student at Halloween bash — before his sister helps nab him
articles.summary: Omar Perez's sister identified him using police photos and the family's Life360 app after the University of Colorado Boulder student's killing.
articles.body: Colorado police have identified the people sought in security footage released after a Halloween party shooting that killed a University of Colorado Boulder student, as prosecutors consider additional charges. On Thursday, Boulder Police Public Information Officer Dionne Waugh confirmed to Fox News Digital that "everyone in the photos and video we released" has now been identified. The primary suspect, Omar Perez, 18, faces murder and related charges in the death of Luca Hanlon, 19, following a deadly confrontation at an off-campus Oct. 31 party in Boulder’s University Hill neighborhood. MASS SHOOTING AT GEORGIA BLOCK PARTY LEAVES 2 DEAD, 35 INJURED After the arrest, detectives asked for the public's help in identifying three other people seen in video and photos from that night, including two males, one wearing an "Art the Clown" shirt and another in a red hoodie, and a female witness. It’s unclear whether they will face charges. "The investigation is ongoing. When and if there are additional arrests or charges, I will send out a news release," Waugh said. Shannon Carbone, the public information officer (PIO) for the Boulder County District Attorney’s Office, told Fox News Digital that prosecutors "successfully argued in court Tuesday to have Perez held without bond." Perez's preliminary hearing is scheduled for Feb. 10, 2027, according to the District Attorney's Office. The Colorado Public Defender’s Office declined to comment on the case. The university did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TEEN PREVIOUSLY CONVICTED IN SHOOTING ACCUSED OF KILLING PREGNANT MOM OF 4 INSIDE SPIRIT HALLOWEEN The shooting According to a Boulder police arrest affidavit, police first responded to a home off Marine Street around 9:58 p.m. on Halloween after receiving a noise complaint. Responding officers issued a nuisance-party citation, and hundreds of people left the gathering. Around 90 minutes later, at 11:28 p.m., officers returned after a call concerning gunshots fired. Witnesses told authorities that Perez had been in the group of people that left, but he returned to the residence with six others. They were asked to leave, but Perez and his group allegedly became irate, leading to a scuffle in the living room and on the front porch. A witness said Perez appeared to be wearing a SWAT uniform and a "Purge" mask. A resident at the home put Perez in a headlock, prompting Perez to allegedly pull out a gun and open fire, the affidavit stated. One witness told police he heard Perez threaten, "Oh, I could shoot this place up." POLICE IDENTIFY AGENT KILLED AFTER SUSPECT OPENS FIRE NEAR COLORADO BUS, WOUNDS OTHER 3 OFFICERS Perez shot Hanlon in the neck and another 19-year-old student in the leg. Hanlon died the following day at Boulder Community Health. "I do not have any other updates on the second victim because of privacy. If that changes I will send out a news release," Waugh told Fox News Digital. Sister identifies suspect The arrest affidavit stated that Perez’s sister saw photos released by Boulder police and contacted them after recognizing her brother's clothes. She then checked the family's "Life360" app, which tracked Perez arriving at the residence around the time of the shooting. The app also mapped his path following the shooting. Over the next several hours, Perez allegedly traveled through Westminster, Arvada, Keenesburg, and then back to Thornton. "The defendant was arrested in Thornton. He is not a CU student and, contrary to some rumors, was not arrested on campus," Carbone told Fox News Digital. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X His sister told investigators that days before the shooting, Perez illegally purchased a 10mm Glock "on the street" and posted photos of the weapon on Instagram. She said he had replaced a revolver he "threw in some bushes" after accidentally shooting himself in the calf on Sept. 26. The affidavit also noted that Perez and other people who accompanied him traveled in a newer red Audi sedan. When Perez picked his sister up from work, she got into the Audi and noticed a "black purge looking mask" on the floorboard. She also told police three people were in the vehicle with Perez. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Perez allegedly told his sister that they had been beaten up earlier at a party they attended, "by four guys and his friends," the affidavit stated. In addition to murder with extreme indifference, Perez faces first-degree assault and attempted first-degree murder charges, both with extreme indifference. "For first degree murder, the only sentence allowed under law is life in prison without the possibility of parole. Additional charges will likely be filed," Carbone said. Luca Hanlon CU Boulder identified Hanlon, of Pennsylvania, as a second-year media production student in its College of Communication, Media, Design and Information. "It doesn't feel real. He was my best friend. He was always there. If I needed a shoulder to cry, he was there, to celebrate the biggest wins in life. He was just like an all-around, stand-up, great, just model citizen," Hanlon’s friend, Jack Anderson, told Denver’s ABC 7. "I would say he was who I aspired to be in life. He was that person." Anyone with any information about the case is urged to contact Boulder police at 303-441-3333, or submit tips online at the police department’s Evidence Submission Portal.

articles.title: 'Incredible' Isles of Scilly women celebrated in new display
articles.summary: The display features the stories of 60 women who live in the Isles of Scilly.
articles.body:
A new exhibition is celebrating the lives and voices of women in the Isles of Scilly.

No Woman is an Island features the stories of 60 women, from young women to some of archipelago's oldest residents.

It brings together portraits, quotes, five suitcase installations created by island artists and a 25-minute film featuring the voices of women who live there. The free exhibition will be on display in the Isles of Scilly Steamship Office in Hugh Town, St Mary's, until summer 2027.

Artistic director of Scary Little Girls Rebecca Mordan said: "There are a disproportionate number of incredible women here - there must be something in the water."

The exhibition was put together by the Isles of Scilly Museum and Cultural Centre and feminist production company Scary Little Girls, with support of the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

It draws on more than 18 months of work with women across the islands with stories gathered through recorded interviews and shared community events.

Museum director Lydia Bassett said: "The new museum will be filled with amazing stories from across the islands, but there are a lot of bold sea captains, heroic gig rowers, lighthouse keepers and rescuers... we wanted to put Scilly's women front and centre."

The stories gathered through the project will also form a permanent display in the new Isles of Scilly Museum and Cultural Centre, which is being developed in the restored Grade II-listed Town Hall in Hugh Town and is due to open in June 2027.

articles.title: Age of consent: Pat McFadden says changes to law will be discussed after Brand allegations
articles.summary: A woman who alleges she was raped by the jailed comedian when she was 16 is campaigning to see relationships between 16-and 17-year-olds and adults made illegal.
articles.body:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings.

She told the paper she was "devastated" by the decision and that police had said they didn't want the trial "to become 'the Alice show'", a reference to her pseudonym in the stories published in 2023.

It is understood the Met Police has apologised for the language officers used in a meeting with Latter about her case.

A Met spokesperson said: "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pension secretary, told Kuenssberg that it was worth debating a change to age of consent laws.

Whately said she has teenage daughters and would be concerned if they brought home a man many years older than them.

"I think any parent would look twice," she said, adding: "Let's have the debate."

Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC charity, said 16 and 17-year-olds can be particularly vulnerable to grooming by some adults and laws have been changed in recent years to prevent more people in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with children of such an age.

She said "other laws are failing to prevent them from being sexually exploited", adding: "Even though they are over the age of consent, young people are still entitled to be protected from harm."

articles.title: Yemen government forces withdraw from area near Bab el Mandeb Strait, Houthis in control
articles.summary: Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognised Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
articles.body: Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognised Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control. The government’s retreat ​from the Bab el Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime chokepoint, creating ‌a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes. The Bab el Mandeb Strait is one ​of the world’s most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly ​from Asia to Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal. The southern Yemeni forces said they were ⁠redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, ​including the capital Sanaa and Yemen’s most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control. “The Southern ​Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the southern forces said in a statement. “This step is taken based on the priority of securing the ​capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.” Government ​forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south ‌in September ⁠in an attempt to seize control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el Mandeb. The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 UN-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key US ​ally and the world’s biggest ​crude exporter. Houthi attacks on ⁠the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the nine-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ​ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom’s Red Sea oil ​export hub ⁠of Yanbu. In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Fighting ⁠is intensifying ​around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The ​city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to ​enter, and civilians are unable to leave.

articles.title: Israeli strike in Gaza kills senior Hamas commander
articles.summary: Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip killed a senior leader of the militant group Hamas on Sunday, Israel reported. The Israeli Defense Force (IDF) announced the death of Samir Abu Younis, a commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade — crediting an overnight strike that hit southern Gaza. articles.body:
Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip killed a senior leader of the militant group Hamas on Sunday, Israel reported.

The Israeli Defense Force (IDF) announced the death of Samir Abu Younis, a commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade — crediting an overnight strike that hit southern Gaza.

The statement alleged he “directed terror attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops” and worked “to restore Hamas’ military capabilities.”

“Abu Younis was appointed commander of the brigade approximately 2 months ago, following the elimination of his predecessor,” the IDF continued. “He previously served as the brigade’s deputy commander and commander of the Tel al-Sultan Battalion.”

“The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed,” the Israeli military concluded.

Hamas’s armed wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, similarly confirmed the death on Telegram , writing that Abu Younis was involved in “numerous high-profile operations.” He previously filled the role left behind by Nael Abu Obeid, who was killed by Israeli strikes in September near Rafah, a southern town in the Gaza Strip located near the border of Egypt.

The wing also credited him with helping to oversee and plan the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel — an event that was potentially responsible for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ouster .

Netanyahu’s successor is opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who joined Israel’s emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel. He later resigned over disagreements about the direction of the war.

While on the campaign trail, Eisenkot targeted the former prime minister over security failures that led up to Oct. 7. He advocated for a “formal state commission of inquiry” about the attack, a move Netanyahu has reportedly blocked, according to Anadolu, citing former Israeli intelligence officer Barak Seri.

Seri accused Netanyahu of being warned about the Hamas attack before it happened but “ignored it all.”

Israeli President Isaac Herzog backed Eisenkot to try to form a new government, but the new potential leader has struggled to build the necessary coalition to take power. Eisenkot has refused to work with the Arab parties who disagree with him on his campaign promise to label Hamas a “ terrorist group .”

articles.title: Millions pledged for Hadrian's Wall tourism push
articles.summary: More than £5.5m will be used to modernise tourist infrastructure in Northumberland and Cumbria.
articles.body:
Plans to spend more than £5.7m in an effort to attract thousands more people to Hadrian's Wall have been agreed.

The Borderlands Partnership - a coalition of five local authorities in Northern England and Southern Scotland - said the money would be used to transform visitor infrastructure along the Roman structure through Northumberland and Cumbria.

It is hoped the investment will draw 780,000 more tourists annually and generate £86.1m in additional spending.

Among the key improvements will be a 1.2 mile (1.94km) cycle route along the Military Road, connecting a number of attractions directly to the wall including the Reivers Trails network and Kielder Water and Forest Park.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , visitor access will also be modernised with new physical and digital "information hubs" across 42 locations along the entire length of the wall in Northumberland.

Mark Mather, deputy chairman of the Northumberland National Park and Conservative county councillor, said the funding would "make a huge difference".

"Hadrian's Wall is absolutely integral to not only Northumberland National Park but the North East as a whole," he said.

"It is one of our most important landmarks."

Northumberland County Council leader Glen Sanderson described the investment as "a landmark moment".

"By directly connecting Hadrian's Wall to Kielder Forest, Haltwhistle and our wider active networks, we are removing barriers for visitors and modernising one of the UK's most iconic historic assets," he said.

In Cumbria, the Discover Hadrian's Wall West project will introduce 68 heritage-themed interpretation points and physical and digital wayfinding across 10 trail locations.

Lady Jane Gibson, chair of the Hadrian's Wall WHS Partnership Board, said the money would be "transformational for Hadrian's Wall and how we can better serve communities and visitors".

"The World Heritage Site in some areas can be hidden in the landscape so the stories that the Wall can tell are waiting to be told."

articles.title: Meet Chris Qian, the Virginia teen who started ReTech for Kids at 14, helped distribute 2,000 refurbished devices with over 100 youth volunteers, won a $5,000 pitch prize and earned a 2026 Diana Award
articles.summary: Chris Qian was only 14 when he founded ReTech for Kids, a nonprofit that collects, refurbishes, and redistributes second-hand technology to
articles.body: Chris Qian was only 14 when he founded ReTech for Kids, a nonprofit that collects, refurbishes, and redistributes second-hand technology to under-resourced students across the United States. Three years later, the initiative has mobilised more than 100 youth volunteers, helped distribute 2,000 refurbished devices, and earned Qian a $5,000 prize at the University of Vermont’s 2026 Vermont Pitch Challenge, according to the Diana Award Roll of Honour, UVM, and MIT Solve.Qian’s work began with a simple observation: many students do not have reliable access to a personal computer, while usable devices are often discarded or left unused. Rather than treating that as an unavoidable reality, he built a system that turns unwanted electronics into practical learning tools for young people who need them most. Read more about his work, as per the reports, here:The problem he sawReTech for Kids was created to address the digital divide, a gap that affects students who lack reliable access to devices, internet, or the skills needed to use them. According to the organisation’s MIT Solve profile, UNICEF estimates that about 1.3 billion children ages 3 to 18 worldwide do not have reliable access to personal devices.That gap has consequences beyond homework. Students without their own computer may struggle to attend virtual classes, complete assignments, learn coding, or explore interests such as video editing that require capable hardware.Qian’s solution is to give those students fully functioning devices rather than asking them to buy new ones. For many recipients, the donated computer is their first personal computer, which makes the difference even more significant.How the nonprofit worksReTech for Kids collects devices through partnerships with businesses and community centres. Student volunteers then diagnose, repair, and upgrade each device, replacing hard drives with SSDs, increasing RAM, cleaning internal components, and testing keyboards, batteries, and displays.The organisation also uses lightweight Linux distributions to make older devices usable, since they can run well on hardware that may no longer support Windows or macOS. Qian is developing a modified version of Linux Mint XFCE called ReTechOS, designed specifically for students and first-time computer owners.Once a device passes quality checks, ReTech for Kids partners with other nonprofits to identify students most in need. Devices are delivered with basic digital literacy guides and, where possible, access to ongoing technical support.The impact so farOver three years, Qian has led more than 100 youth volunteers and helped distribute 2,000 refurbished devices. The Diana Award Roll of Honour describes the initiative as combining environmental responsibility with educational opportunity, since it diverts unwanted electronics away from landfills while putting them into the hands of students.That dual benefit is part of what makes the model compelling. A laptop that might otherwise be thrown away becomes a tool for learning, and a student who might otherwise be excluded from digital opportunities gains a way to participate.The work has also given young volunteers a role in the process. They are not just recipients of a service, they are the people collecting, repairing, and distributing the devices, which builds both technical skills and a sense of ownership.Recognition from UVMQian’s work earned second place in the 2026 Vermont Pitch Challenge, a Shark Tank-like competition for high school entrepreneurs. He received a $5,000 prize for ReTech for Kids, which was described by UVM as a nonprofit that refurbishes and donates laptops and other devices to K-12 students to close the digital divide and reduce e-waste.The competition drew more than 100 teams from 24 U.S. states, with five finalist teams invited to pitch in person at UVM on April 7, 2026. Qian’s placement among that group reflects both the strength of the idea and the clarity with which he presented it.The prize money is not just a reward. It is also a signal that the work is being taken seriously by judges, educators, and entrepreneurs who see the value in a student-led solution to a real-world problem.The Diana AwardIn 2026, Qian was also named a recipient of the Diana Award, an honour that recognises young people for their social action and humanitarian work. The Roll of Honour describes him as someone who has demonstrated the ability to inspire and mobilise others to create long-lasting change.The award highlights Qian’s ability to combine practical action with a broader vision. He is not only distributing devices, he is building a model that others can replicate, using volunteers, partnerships, and refurbished technology to address a persistent inequality.At 17, Qian is already being recognised alongside young leaders from around the world. That recognition reflects the scale of what he has built, even though the organisation began with a single student’s concern about access to technology.Why the work mattersThe digital divide is not just a technology issue, it is an education and opportunity issue. Students who lack access to devices may fall behind in school, miss out on digital skills, and face barriers when they enter the workforce.ReTech for Kids addresses that problem at its source. By refurbishing and redistributing devices, Qian is creating a practical, scalable way to put technology into the hands of students who need it most.The initiative also shows how young people can lead on issues that adults often struggle to solve. Qian saw a gap, built a solution, recruited volunteers, and earned recognition from multiple institutions, all before finishing high school.What comes nextQian’s work is ongoing. ReTech for Kids continues to collect, refurbish, and distribute devices, and the organisation is developing ReTechOS to make its devices even more accessible to first-time computer users.The combination of a $5,000 prize, a Diana Award, and a growing volunteer network suggests the initiative has momentum. What began as a student-led effort to close a gap has become a model that could expand further, reaching more students and diverting more devices from landfills.For Qian, the goal is simple. Technology should not be a barrier to learning, and a device that still works should not end up in a landfill when it could help a student build a future.You use AI every day. articles.title: From battlefield drones to bigger guns: China upgrades Pakistan-used VT-4 tank
articles.summary: China has developed an upgraded version of its VT-4 main battle tank, a key component of Pakistan's armoured fleet.
articles.body: China has developed an upgraded version of its VT-4 main battle tank, a key component of Pakistan's armoured fleet.The latest upgrade incorporates stronger armour, improved sensors and a larger weapon station designed to counter emerging battlefield threats, according to a report by the South China Morning Post (SCMP).The new variant, believed to be designated VT-4B, is expected to be displayed at the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai from December 7 to 13. Images circulating on social media show the tank arriving at the southern Chinese city alongside other military equipment ahead of the biennial event.The upgrades mark a significant departure from the existing VT-4A configuration, although the new tank retains the overall design characteristics of a third-generation main battle tank, SCMP reported.The VT-4 is primarily an export tank and has entered service with the armies of Pakistan, Thailand and Nigeria. It is among China's most successful armoured vehicle exports.30mm gun, stronger armour to counter drone threatsOne of the most visible changes to the VT-4B is the addition of a 30mm remotely operated weapon station, replacing the standard 12.7mm roof-mounted machine gun fitted on most Chinese tanks.According to SCMP, the larger gun is intended to provide greater firepower against loitering munitions and first-person-view (FPV) drones, as well as infantry and anti-tank teams.The tank also appears to have received substantial armour reinforcement. Images show thicker explosive reactive armour covering the front hull and sides, extending further down to protect the lower front section and parts of the running gear.The upgraded variant is also fitted with an active protection system that appears to be China's GL-6, which is used on newer People's Liberation Army tanks. The system features four phased-array radar panels mounted on the turret for 360-degree threat detection, along with two interceptor launchers near the rear of the turret.Improved sensors and battlefield connectivityThe VT-4B's situational awareness equipment has also been upgraded. Its commander's sight appears to have been replaced by a separately mounted electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR) sensor pod.SCMP reported that comparable sensor systems on advanced Chinese tanks feature automated target acquisition and image recognition, although the precise capabilities of the equipment fitted to the export variant have not been confirmed.The tank's communications antennas have also been replaced with thicker, stick-type models that can support high-bandwidth data links. This could improve communication between vehicles and allow the tank to connect more effectively with other units on the battlefield.Images also show a small radio-frequency array mounted on one side of the remotely operated weapon station. Its function remains unclear. Military observers cited by SCMP have suggested that it could be an independent fire-control radar or a compact high-power microwave emitter designed to disable incoming drones alongside the tank's interceptor system.What the upgrade means for PakistanThe VT-4 is an important part of Pakistan's military equipment acquired from China. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's (SIPRI) Arms Transfers Database 2022, Pakistan signed a contract to acquire 679 VT-4 tanks, which were to be assembled and produced under licence in the country under the name Haider.Subsequent reports said the Pakistan Army had inducted the tank, although its operational capabilities have yet to be tested. It remains unclear whether Islamabad will seek to acquire the upgraded VT-4B variant.Pakistan's Army, Air Force and Navy currently rely heavily on Chinese weapon systems. SIPRI estimates suggest that around 80% of the country's military equipment comes from China.The VT-4B's appearance ahead of the Zhuhai exhibition highlights China's effort to incorporate technologies developed for its newer armoured vehicles into equipment aimed at overseas buyers. However, the extent to which the upgrades will be offered to existing export customers, including Pakistan, remains uncertain.

articles.title: Virginia parents charged after house party draws hundreds of teens, fireworks and alleged underage drinking
articles.summary: Fairfax County police charged Lisa and Aubrey Vaughan after their 13-year-old sons' small backyard party spiraled into a massive gathering with fireworks and crowds.
articles.body: A Virginia couple who say they wanted to give their 13-year-old sons a safe place to hang out with a handful of classmates ended up facing criminal charges after their backyard gathering exploded into a massive party with hundreds of teenagers, fireworks and police descending on their neighborhood. Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance after Fairfax County police responded to their McLean home on Nov. 6. The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older students. "There will be no more," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5 DC, referring to the party for their sons. "We're done." COLLEGE HOMECOMING PARTY TURNS TO CHAOS AS DECK COLLAPSES, LEAVING AT LEAST 28 PEOPLE INJURED Police responded to multiple 911 calls around 9:03 p.m. reporting an out-of-control party. Callers estimated between 100 and 300 people had gathered at the home, where responding officers encountered a large crowd and fireworks being discharged, according to police. Aubrey Vaughan apologized to neighbors, saying he was "embarrassed" by how quickly the gathering spiraled out of control. He and his wife even had their 13-year-old sons go door-to-door to apologize after police dispersed the crowd, according to FOX 5. The couple had planned a small eighth-grade gathering, but the invitation circulated on Snapchat and eventually reached students at a local high school, attracting uninvited teenagers, according to the family's attorney. Aubrey Vaughan said he had "zero idea" high schoolers would show up and that he and his wife struggled to keep them out of their backyard and home. Police described the gathering as an "underage drinking party," but Vaughan disputed suggestions that alcohol was permitted. He told FOX 5 that the invitation explicitly prohibited alcohol and bags, and that he and his wife were home supervising the entire time. Aubrey Vaughan estimated the incident lasted about 45 minutes, saying he realized things were getting out of hand roughly 10 to 15 minutes before officers arrived. "They wanted to maintain a safe place, free from alcohol, for kids to have a good time, but they had no control about all the kids that arrived and caused chaos in their neighborhood," the couple's attorney, Alaric Piette, told FOX 5. Piette said the parents welcomed officers and offered to let them inspect the party area, but police declined. Both parents later turned themselves in and were released on $1,000 unsecured bonds each. FAMILIES CONFRONT CALIFORNIA 'PARTY MOM' IN COURT, CALLING HER A 'MONSTER' WHO GROOMED THEIR CHILDREN Fairfax County Police Chief Kevin Davis acknowledged the challenges parents face when deciding whether to host gatherings at home rather than let teenagers socialize elsewhere without supervision. "I think it's universally a bad idea to host anything at a home," Davis said, warning that large gatherings involving alcohol, drugs or reckless behavior can quickly become dangerous. The police chief emphasized that "parents have to be parents" and "adults have to be adults," warning that good intentions can have unintended consequences. Aubrey Vaughan, meanwhile, said he was grateful police helped disperse the crowd and harbors no resentment toward the responding officers. "The lesson is just make sure you're watching Snapchat," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5. articles.title: US floated idea swapping Ukrainian territory for NATO membership: Zelensky
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said U.S. negotiators floated the possibility of Ukraine surrendering in the eastern Donbas region and conceding it to Russia in exchange for NATO membership. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky told reporters…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said U.S. negotiators floated the possibility of Ukraine surrendering in the eastern Donbas region and conceding it to Russia in exchange for NATO membership.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky told reporters Friday.

Zelensky said Ukraine would not simply surrender its territory to Russia but suggested he could put the proposal before the Ukrainian people if the U.S. and its allies offered sufficient security guarantees.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” he said. “I have no right to make that decision on my own. But we need specifics, and we don’t have them yet.”

Russia has occupied much of Ukraine’s Donbas region since the start of the war four years ago, and has been a major point of contention throughout negotiations to end the war.

The Ukrainian leader said any potential agreement would need to include a strong Ukrainian military, adequate weapons and financial assistance, and security guarantees from NATO and the European Union.

He said he had told U.S. negotiators that protections modeled on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense provision would be the “absolute minimum” Ukraine could accept. The provision considers an armed attack against one NATO member an attack against all members.

The prospect of Ukraine joining NATO would be a major concession by Russia, which has long opposed the country’s membership in the military alliance. Russian President Vladimir Putin has cited NATO’s potential expansion as part of the justification for launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia occupies much of the region, which encompasses the Donetsk and Luhansk provinces, but Ukrainian forces continue to hold territory there.

Zelensky’s remarks follow two days of U.S.-brokers peace talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi last week, mediated by President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff.

In a Saturday post on the social platform X , Kushner said “several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored,” though he did not directly address the potential exchange of territory for NATO membership.

“NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security,” he wrote. “Any final agreement must be agreed to by the relevant parties, and President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine’s and Europe’s security and make future conflict less likely.”

articles.title: Three ships struck by drones in Black Sea near Romanian shipping canal, PM says
articles.summary: Drones have ​struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal, Prime ‌Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice.
articles.body: BUCHAREST — Drones have ​struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal, Prime ‌Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice. Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships’ crews had managed to control the fires ​on board after the strikes late on Saturday. A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ​ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war ⁠between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance ​in the Black Sea. The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane that links ​the Danube River to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports. Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia’s war in Ukraine. “These ​incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. “They reflect the ​deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.” Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbours with drones. Oprea ‌said ⁠the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the ​Sulina canal, the defence ​ministry said, inside Romanian ⁠territorial waters. Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television ​station Digi24 said the vessel was the Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa ​1. “On Tuesday ⁠and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers,” Oprea said. “We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through ⁠equipment for ​counter-drone warfare.” France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols ​aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement. Many of the ships hit in October and November were anchored near ​or sailing to or from the Sulina canal.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: What big tech’s weekend from hell means for the future of data centers
articles.summary: Microsoft Outlook's Thursday shutdown and the FAA's Friday flight grounding highlight why data center advocates say this infrastructure is essential.
articles.body: The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong. These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives. In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park. INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE' In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison. This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum. In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm. This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial. FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs. This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers. Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed. It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers. For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With the midterms behind us and our tech infrastructure on thin ice, now is the time for the case to be made that, one way or another, our future lies in data centers.

articles.title: Israel kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza two months after killing his predecessor as ceasefire stagnates
articles.summary: Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place.
articles.body: Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight Saturday, both Hamas and the IDF said. Abu Younis, who was a long-time member of the brigade, had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, the previous commander who was killed in a strike in September. And Abu Obeid himself replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, another commander of the Rafah Brigade who was killed in May 2025. The strike comes just days after an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in what the IDF said was an attempt to kill another Hamas commander. In a statement, Hamas’ military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, acknowledged the death of Abu Younis, saying he had joined the brigade in 1991 and was “among the most prominent commanders who participated in planning and overseeing” the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. “The IDF continues to eliminate Hamas leaders in Gaza, and another one joins his predecessors in the depths of hell,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. “The offensive policy that I am leading together with the Prime Minister and the IDF in Gaza will continue – until Gaza is demilitarized and there is no Hamas.” The killing of Abu Younis underscores an emerging pattern in Gaza. Despite a nominal ceasefire that went into effect more than one year ago, Israel has continued to carry out strikes targeting members of Hamas, particularly senior commanders. But those commanders are quickly replaced as Hamas entrenches its own grip on power over the half of Gaza not occupied by Israel. Meanwhile, the Board of Peace, a body created by the Trump administration with United Nations backing to oversee the Gaza ceasefire plan, remains sidelined, unable to make any substantive progress on the 20-point plan agreed to in October 2025. On Friday, the board said it had held “very constructive discussions” with 17 countries about a civilian Gaza police force under the authority of a Palestinian technocratic committee that was supposed to run Gaza. But that committee has yet to enter the enclave, and an international security force meant to stabilize Gaza has yet to materialize. The IDF strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Palestinian officials. The strike hit the hospital’s surgery unit, killing Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy who was awaiting surgery. A total of 40 others were injured in the strike, including two doctors who were in critical condition, officials said. In a statement, the IDF said it had targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” But when pressed on whether Abu Ismail was killed in the strike, the IDF did not answer. Doctors Without Borders (Médicins Sans Frontières, or MSF) condemned the strike, saying: “It is unconscionable that patients and medical staff are once again being killed and injured inside a hospital, a place where lives should be saved, not taken.” MSF withdrew its own staff from the hospital in January because of the presence of armed men inside, as well as concerns over the hospital’s neutrality and management. “Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” MSF said. The Board of Peace also urged both Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 people have been killed in near-daily Israeli strikes in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed one year ago. The shattered territory also faces an unfolding humanitarian crisis ahead of the onset of winter. Last week, seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced. Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it has refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale clean-up and rubble removal efforts. “The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.

articles.title: A sheep that escaped capture for 45 days in Wadsworth, Ohio, was finally caught by 13-year-old Reagan Crumpler, who chased it on horseback and used her roping skills; the animal is now staying at a farm sanctuary
articles.summary: If you thought sheep detectives were only a thing in children's stories, Wadsworth, Ohio, recently had its own real-life investigation.
articles.body: If you thought sheep detectives were only a thing in children's stories, Wadsworth, Ohio, recently had its own real-life investigation. For 45 days, residents, volunteers and animal rescuers followed sightings, searched fields and tried to track down one particularly elusive sheep. The case finally came to an end when a 13-year-old girl arrived on horseback, with a rope and some rather impressive roping skills.The sheep, an American Blackbelly, had been wandering around Wadsworth for over a month as reported by News5 Cleavland, appearing in different parts of the city before disappearing whenever someone tried to approach her. What began as a few unusual sightings soon turned into a community-wide rescue mission, with residents keeping watch and sharing updates in the hope of bringing the animal to safety.The effort was led by Janine Smalley, founder of Whispering Acres Farm Animal Sanctuary, and volunteer Rebecca Roxberry. Their involvement began after a Wadsworth homeowner contacted Roxberry about what she believed was a goat wandering around her yard. A photograph soon cleared up the confusion. The animal was, in fact, an American Blackbelly sheep.Roxberry began feeding the sheep, hoping that regular visits would make it easier to approach her. But the animal had other plans. Every time the rescuers tried to get close, she would bolt, leaving them to start their search all over again. The team received several reports of sightings, but locating the sheep and actually catching her proved to be two very different challenges.Over the following weeks, the rescue effort grew considerably. Volunteers tried using food to lure the sheep, bringing another sheep and a goat into the picture, and even attempting to corner her. The Medina County SPCA and local authorities also joined the search. At one point, a drone was used to track her movements from above and help guide her towards an area where volunteers could reach her.There was growing concern about the animal's safety. She had been spotted crossing busy roads, including State Route 94, several times, and rescuers worried that she could be struck by a passing vehicle. Meanwhile, the community had become increasingly invested in the search. A Facebook event titled 'Catching the Wadsworth Sheep' brought residents together, with people sharing sightings, offering assistance and keeping an eye out for the runaway.Despite the attention, the sheep remained difficult to catch. That was until the rescuers realised they needed someone with a rather different set of skills.A call for help seeking an experienced roper eventually caught the attention of Shannon Crumpler, whose daughter Reagan had been attending roping lessons several times a week. Shannon was confident that her daughter could help, and put her forward for the job. At just 13, Reagan was already comfortable around horses and had been developing her roping abilities over the preceding months.On November 11, Reagan headed out with her horse, Catalena, affectionately called Cat, to attempt the capture. What followed was a chase that lasted a couple of hours.The pair pursued the sheep across a field bordering US Route 224 in Wadsworth. However, the animal was not particularly interested in being rescued. Each time Reagan and Cat got close enough to attempt a rope capture, the sheep would change direction, leaving Reagan to try again. The chase continued as Reagan updated her mother over the phone about their whereabouts.At one point, the young roper began to lose hope. But she encouraged Cat to keep going, and the horse seemed to respond by picking up the pace. The pair eventually managed to get ahead of the sheep, giving Reagan the opportunity she had been waiting for. Her roping skills finally paid off, and the elusive animal was caught.The news brought an emotional end to a search that had involved dozens of people. Roxberry recalled that volunteers were moved to tears when they realised the sheep was finally safe. After 45 days of sightings, failed attempts and repeated searches, they could finally breathe a little easier.The sheep was named Gerri Reagan, in honour of the teenager who helped bring her in. She was taken to Whispering Acres Farm Animal Sanctuary, where she is now settling into what Smalley described as a 'princess palace'. The animal is reportedly doing well, although she was found to be a little underweight after her extended time roaming outdoors.Her recovery will involve a gradual refeeding programme and a veterinary examination to check for injuries and parasites. The sanctuary has also placed her on a 72-hour hold, giving anyone who can provide legal documentation of ownership an opportunity to claim her. If nobody comes forward, she is expected to remain at the sanctuary indefinitely.For Reagan, the experience was about more than successfully putting her roping lessons to use. She was happy knowing that the sheep would have somewhere safe to stay and receive proper care. Asked whether she would take part in another animal rescue, she did not hesitate: she would do it again in a heartbeat.The rescue also had an unexpected ripple effect. The sanctuary gained six new volunteers following the story, while the people of Wadsworth got a reminder of what a community can accomplish when everyone decides to look out for one small, wandering animal.After 45 days on the run, Gerri Reagan's great escape is finally over. And while she may not have been particularly keen on being caught, she now has a safe place to call home, thanks to a determined teenager, a very capable horse and a town that refused to give up looking for her.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran raises stakes with new drone attacks as Trump signals a waiting game
articles.summary: Gulf states have been worried for weeks that Iran may again begin to target them in an effort to force a resolution to the nine-month regional conflict on its terms.
articles.body: Gulf states have been worried for weeks that Iran may again begin to target them in an effort to force a resolution to the nine-month regional conflict on its terms. In the last few days, that anxiety has deepened with two attempted drone attacks on Bahrain, an American ally which hosts major US military facilities, while Tehran has also warned the Gulf states not to “reopen old wounds.” Iran appears to be raising the stakes as it struggles to prevent more Gulf oil and gas from getting through the Strait of Hormuz and as its economy labors under the United States’ blockade and the cumulative effect of international sanctions. The Bahrain Defense Force said Sunday it had “intercepted and destroyed” several Iranian drones, after a similar interception on Friday. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had earlier claimed an attack on a US helicopter base in Bahrain. CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment. The targeting of Bahrain has accompanied a more belligerent tone out of Tehran – towards Iran’s neighbors, the consequences of renewed US or Israeli strikes and the state of negotiations with the US. Iran was incensed by suggestions from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) last week that it would have to pay its neighbors compensation for attacks on their territory, something Iran itself is seeking in any deal with the US. “How can countries that actively participated in military aggression against a neighbouring country and made their airspace, territory and waters available to those who attacked Iranian territory speak of seeking compensation from Iran?” asked foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei in a news conference on Sunday. “What about Iran’s inherent and legal right to defend itself?” In a reminder that Iran does not forget the past, Baghaei said the Gulf states “must be careful not to reopen old wounds,” referring to their support for Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in the war with Iran in the 1980s. Iran wants the Gulf states “to pay the price for a war they did not choose, then give up their right to accountability and compensation. This is an equation that cannot be accepted,” said Ebtesam Al-Ketbi, of the Emirates Policy Center think tank, on Sunday. Shipping attacks A sign of growing unease about the prospect of renewed hostilities came last week when the GCC announced an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for its unified military command and the deployment of forces to the facility. The organization’s secretary general, Jasem Mohamed Al Budaiwi, said the move showed “a firm Gulf commitment to safeguarding the security and sovereignty of the GCC states” following what he called “heinous Iranian attacks.” Iran has also stepped up attacks on shipping in the Gulf, with almost daily claims – few of them substantiated – that tankers have struck mines as they’ve tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz. For Tehran, the increase in Gulf energy exports to close to pre-war levels in recent weeks, and the sharp decline in oil prices, deprive it of vital leverage in negotiations. The International Energy Agency said Gulf oil exports - excluding Oman - reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, about 26% below prewar levels. At the same time, Iran has been unable to export any meaningful amount of its own crude for more than two months. The Iranian regime is demanding an end to the US blockade, the progressive removal of international sanctions and an unfreezing of billions of dollars in frozen assets as conditions for resuming negotiations with the US. But US President Donald Trump appears content to let the economic squeeze on Iran take its course, anticipating that Tehran will have to soften its terms and recognizing the Gulf states want to avoid another round of conflict. “At the request of the nations that I am ⁠looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump said Thursday. At the same time, he canceled efforts by Vice President JD Vance to resurrect talks with Iran, declaring: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.” An unstable limbo Indeed, Iran’s economic pain appears to be deepening even as senior officials in Tehran insist it can withstand the pressure and can access hard currency to support the rial, whose value has fallen drastically since the conflict began. One perpetual sign of hardship is the long lines seen at gas stations in many parts of Iran. Esmail Saghab Esfahani, a vice president, admitted last week that there was a supply problem and that Iranians could no longer count on fuel stations to cover what they need. Some residents of the port city of Bandar Abbas blocked traffic on Thursday to protest against petrol shortages. The speaker of the Iranian parliament, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested officials stop talking about the fuel issue, always sensitive in Iran. And yet there are no public indications the regime is ready to compromise. Baghaei was asked Sunday whether Iran would accept a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment or a reduction in enrichment levels in negotiations with Washington. “No. We are not at that stage at all. During this period, we are not discussing any details related to the nuclear issue, nor have we held any such discussions.” Ghalibaf said Sunday it made no difference whether Washington wanted negotiations or war. “If the Americans make another mistake this time, the capabilities and will of Iran’s armed forces will determine the geography of the battlefield.” Iran has frequently warned that another chapter in the conflict will see it broaden targets to infrastructure across the region, including subsea cables. Additionally, its Houthi allies in Yemen fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia almost daily and appear to have put Saudi-backed government forces under renewed pressure in the south of Yemen, forcing them to retreat from near the Red Sea in a setback in their campaign. The result is an unstable limbo across the region. “The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security,” wrote Israeli analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies on X. The US “cannot assume that time alone will force Tehran to surrender. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what its leadership considers fundamental national interests.”
