articles.title: America's first Muslim senator exposes a political blind spot
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's election as the first Muslim senator-elect puts Islamism, the Muslim Brotherhood and antisemitism at the heart of a national debate.
articles.body: As a Muslim woman, physician and longtime critic of Islamism, I have witnessed firsthand the consequences of extremist interpretations of my faith. I have examined the bodies of Jews murdered by Hamas during the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel; recorded the testimony of Yazidi and Kurdish victims of ISIS atrocities in Iraq; interviewed children inducted into ISIS and the Taliban; consoled Christians persecuted in Iraq and Pakistan; and walked through the now-dismantled Al Hol detention camp in Syria. I know deeply the tragedies promulgated by practitioners of my faith who believe in an extremist interpretation of the religion called Islamism or political Islam. I also know there is a rising tide of people who don’t differentiate between the two and believe all Islam is extremist. 'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS WARN EL-SAYED TO TONE DOWN 'CONDESCENSION' ON MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD QUESTIONS Islamism and anti-Muslim bigotry took center stage in the midterm elections, which delivered the nation’s first Muslim senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich. Yet both political parties are challenged in meeting this moment. Republicans too often fail to distinguish Muslims from Islamists, while Democrats seem unwilling to examine the distinction at all. Accusations of "Islamophobia," amplified by the politics of identity and "anti-racism," have further obscured a debate Americans urgently need to have. Too often, Islamophobia is conflated with anti-Muslim xenophobia to the detriment of Muslim critics of Islamism who seek to expose Islamist influence and to the benefit of Islamist ideology and its allies. Expect accusations of Islamophobia to be increasingly deployed as a means of diverting scrutiny away from El-Sayed, whose senatorial bid exposed these tensions. During a television interview, El-Sayed denied that his family was connected to the Muslim Brotherhood. After the election, he joked about the allegations, mocking his critics. ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES The danger of Islamist entryism Republicans frequently mishandled the issue. Vice President JD Vance called El-Sayed "very, very evil." President Donald Trump repeatedly labeled him a "jihadist." Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., made sweeping statements questioning Muslims’ fitness for political office. Such attacks risk alienating Muslim voters and undermining legitimate scrutiny of El-Sayed’s political associations, statements and policy positions. Republicans will continue to struggle with these questions until they understand how Islamism covertly exploits democratic institutions and electoral politics — a challenge identified overseas. A 2025 French government report on the Muslim Brotherhood examined "Islamist entryism," or Muslim Brotherhood efforts to build influence through local institutions, associations and political structures. EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE Democrats’ ‘Islamophobia' blind spot Republicans are not alone in their failure to distinguish Islamist political activity from apolitical pluralism. Too often, Democratic leaders dismiss legitimate questions about Islamist ideology as "Islamophobia," even as disputes over antisemitism, anti-Zionism and the Israel-Hamas conflict deepen divisions within their party. Following the midterms, former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel faced questions from Fox News host Brian Kilmeade about rising antisemitism and anti-Israel activism within Democratic politics. His responses illustrated the difficulty party leaders face in confronting these divisions. ‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE Fox News Digital investigative reporter Asra Nomani documented another revealing moment three days after the election, when El-Sayed attended the Arab America Foundation’s national summit where an event leader celebrated El-Sayed’s victory with the declaration, "You destroyed AIPAC twice," before invoking "Free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea." El-Sayed smiled as these remarks were delivered, without publicly challenging them at that moment. The phrase "From the river to the sea" is interpreted by many Israelis and Jews as a call for Israel’s elimination, although some Palestinian advocates claim it is a demand for freedom and equal rights. Such ambiguity makes it all the more important for elected officials to explain what these slogans mean and whether they support Israel’s continued existence as a Jewish state. JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS As an expert on Islamism, I can see how such public celebration raises serious questions about the ideological expectations some supporters already place on El-Sayed. He should answer those questions directly. The same scrutiny should extend to elected officials’ positions on antisemitism, anti-Zionism and American foreign policy toward Israel, Qatar, Turkey and Iran, countries whose relationships with Islamist movements differ substantially but remain important to U.S. national security. Consider Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., who faced questions during a CNN interview about whether he considered Iran an American adversary. His response deserves examination on its merits, particularly considering reporting about his past statements and associations. But such scrutiny must be grounded in verifiable evidence, not assumptions based on a politician’s Muslim identity. That distinction is essential. When all Muslims are portrayed as Islamists, genuine ideological concerns become harder to investigate. When every criticism of political Islam is dismissed as "Islamophobia," the public loses another opportunity for honest debate. El-Sayed’s political alliances under scrutiny El-Sayed’s campaign offers further examples. He appeared alongside far-left commentator Hasan Piker, who previously said America "deserved 9/11," a remark Piker later characterized as inappropriate. Piker has also faced criticism over his commentary about Hamas and the Oct. 7 attacks. El-Sayed subsequently distanced himself from Piker. Politicians shouldn't be held responsible for every statement made by their supporters. But they must be willing to reject extremist rhetoric clearly and consistently, particularly when it comes from influential figures within their own coalitions. El-Sayed also faced criticism over his "hurt people hurt people" remarks following an attack on Temple Israel synagogue in Michigan that federal authorities investigated as a Hezbollah-inspired act of terrorism — remarks he claims were misconstrued. Yet political leaders have a responsibility to condemn antisemitic violence unequivocally, without language that could reasonably be interpreted as legitimizing it. The Muslim Brotherhood question Questions about El-Sayed’s family background and historical associations with Islamist organizations also surfaced during the campaign — allegations involving charities associated with his mother and archived social media statements attributed to his half-sister concerning the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejects any claims that he or his family are Muslim Brotherhood affiliates. More directly relevant are El-Sayed’s published political views. Eitan Fischberger highlighted pro-Islamist 2012 columns co-authored by El-Sayed following Islamist Mohamed Morsi’s election — Egypt’s first democratically elected president, who was ousted in 2013 amid mass protests against his government. El-Sayed had urged recognition of the Brotherhood’s participation in Egypt’s political uprising. Those writings are legitimate subjects for scrutiny. Americans deserve to know whether El-Sayed’s views of the Brotherhood have since changed. MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED Protecting Muslims without protecting Islamism We must distinguish Muslims who support liberal democracy and religious pluralism from those who seek to impose Islamist political principles. We must also distinguish anti-Muslim hatred, discrimination and violence from legitimate criticism of religiously inspired political movements. The two are not interchangeable. When politicians conflate them, they create a climate in which ideological scrutiny becomes more difficult and religious prejudice becomes easier to excuse. Rejecting Islamism isn’t an act of anti-Muslim hatred. For pluralist, anti-Islamist Muslims, it is an affirmation of religious liberty, democratic government, individual rights and the separation of religious authority from state power. A healthy, liberal democracy must protect the right of Muslims to worship, participate in politics and hold public office while also protecting the right of Americans to scrutinize any political ideology, including Islamism. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed should be challenged vigorously on his views of the Muslim Brotherhood, Islamist political movements, antisemitism and Israel’s right to exist. His public appearances, past writings and political alliances provide legitimate starting points for that examination. Americans must not empower politicians who excuse terrorism, defend antisemitic violence or seek to undermine constitutional democracy, regardless of their religion or political party. Both parties should support candidates, including Muslim candidates, who defend democratic pluralism and reject political extremism. The answer to Islamist entryism is neither anti-Muslim prejudice nor silence in the face of extremism. It is informed scrutiny, intellectual honesty and an unwavering commitment to America’s constitutional principles.

articles.title: Two people injured after taxiing planes collide at Miami International Airport
articles.summary: Two taxiing planes collided at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, officials said, a day after a nationwide ground stop disrupted flights across the country.
articles.body: Two taxiing planes collided at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, officials said, a day after a nationwide ground stop disrupted flights across the country. At about 9 p.m. ET Saturday, the wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 as both aircrafts were taxiing, according to a statement from the FAA. The Copa plane was taxiing to the gate, while the UPS plane was departing for Bogota, Colombia, the FAA said. The Copa flight had six crew members and 166 passengers aboard at the time of the collision, according to a statement from the airline. Greg Chin, a spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department, said in a statement that two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries and were not hospitalized. The FAA said air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight. UPS said in a statement that it was aware of the incident and “committed to working with authorities to determine what happened.” “The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority,” the company said. The collision came a day after the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop because of a widespread air traffic control telecommunication issue. The ground stop lasted more than four hours, and led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays. Officials believe a router problem during routine work was the cause of the outage. As of 10:20 a.m. ET Sunday, 1,583 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been cancelled, and another 2,944 were delayed. Last year, 15 people were killed when a UPS cargo plane crashed just outside of Louisville, Kentucky’s Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.

articles.title: A Utah husband-and-wife duo turned their search for unusual sweets during the pandemic into a freeze-dried candy business now selling its treats in more than 500 US stores
articles.summary: A husband-and-wife duo in the United States turned their interest in making people smile into a freeze-dried candy business that has reached more than 500
articles.body: A husband-and-wife duo in the United States turned their interest in making people smile into a freeze-dried candy business that has reached more than 500 stores. Melinna (Mel) and Jesus (Zeus) Macias founded Trendy Treats after the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted their ability to source unusual candies from around the world.Instead of relying on overseas suppliers, they decided to make innovative candies in the US. Its products are now sold through online marketplaces, the company website, and retailers across the country, giving shoppers access to familiar sweets with a different texture. According to Utah’s Own (Department of Agriculture and Food), the idea grew into a business that has reached over one million customers. The business describes its treats as crispy, crunchy, flavourful, and fun.How the COVID-19 pandemic inspired the couple to start Trendy TreatsTrendy Treats was founded by Melinna (Mel) and Jesus (Zeus) Macias, a husband-and-wife team. The company’s account says the idea took shape during the 2019 pandemic, a period when many things felt uncertain. The couple said their passion for making people smile was something they could rely on. Covid-19 also made it difficult for them to source unique candies from around the world.They responded by deciding to manufacture their own products in the United States. The move gave the founders a way to create the unusual sweets they had been unable to obtain. That decision became the starting point for Trendy Treats, which has since developed into a business selling freeze-dried and novelty candies for customers across the country.Trendy Treats turns familiar sweets into crispy, freeze-dried candy creationsTrendy Treats describes itself as a candy company specialising in premium freeze-dried candy. Its products take familiar sweets and turn them into treats that the company describes as crispy, crunchy and flavourful. The range includes different types of freeze-dried candy, from fruity gummies to caramel-flavoured delights. The company says its products are made to give familiar flavours an exciting twist.It highlights quality and innovation as central parts of its approach. The sweets are marketed for snacking, gifting, and sharing, while personalised candy boxes are available for people buying treats as gifts. The listing describes the products as suitable for candy lovers of all ages and for parties or special occasions.How Trendy Treats grew to reach more than 500 stores across the USThe company says its freeze-dried treats are now available in more than 500 stores across the United States. The range suits parties, gifts, and everyday snacking alike. Its Utah’s Own listing names several retailers where customers can find the products, including ItSugar, Harmons, TJ Maxx, HomeGoods, and Marshalls.The company says its creations began attracting attention after it started sharing videos online. Viewers watched, shared, and liked the videos, helping the business go viral. Trendy Treats says this response helped it grow and also gave it opportunities to support communities through donations and collaborations. The listing reports that the brand has reached over one million customers.What makes Trendy Treats’ freeze-dried candies different from regular sweetsTrendy Treats says its mission is to manufacture and sell high-quality freeze-dried and novelty candies. The company presents candy as a way to bring sweetness into people's lives and make the world a better place. Its profile also highlights sharing as part of the brand’s purpose, describing the products as suitable for parties, special occasions, and gifts.Customers can choose from a variety of freeze-dried sweets, including fruity and caramel-flavoured options. The company’s listing includes customer reviews praising its product selection, packaging, delivery, and customer service. Trendy Treats is based in West Valley City, Utah.You use AI every day. articles.title: Estonia to shut its border with Russia, blaming the Kremlin for failed arson attack
articles.summary: Estonia is to close its border with Russia after blaming the Kremlin for a suspected attack on a defense technology company, Estonia’s prime minister said Sunday.
articles.body: Estonia is to close its border with Russia after blaming the Kremlin for a suspected attack on a defense technology company, Estonia’s prime minister said Sunday. Eight people have been detained after allegedly attempting an arson attack on the company overnight on Saturday, authorities say. No one was injured. Estonian security services say the attempted attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU. There has been no initial response from Russia. “If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement Sunday. “Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable,” he added. Border crossings will be closed from 1 December and Michal gave no timescale for when they would reopen.

articles.title: Thousands rally in Czech Republic against state media funding changes
articles.summary: Critics say proposed funding changes will give the government more control of state media.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of the Czech capital to protest against proposed changes to the funding of public service media, which critics fear could weaken broadcaster independence.

Many of the protesters assembled in Letna Park in Prague on Sunday afternoon.

Some of the demonstrators wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers in tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades.

Local authorities anticipated a large crowd days before the November 17 holiday commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution against Communist rule, which propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.

Under the proposed changes introduced last month , the government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis wants to replace the current monthly fee of 205 crowns ($9.45), which is charged to each household, with funding from the state budget.

Opponents say the change will stifle media freedom as it will make the outlets more dependent on the state. The government insists the plan will not affect editorial independence or programme content.

The bill has passed a preliminary vote ⁠⁠in parliament and awaits further debate.

Broadcast workers have been striking against the proposal since June and earlier this month public media employees staged a one-day strike, leading to state media boycotts by artists and students.

The Million Moments for Democracy group organised Sunday’s demonstration and said “Babis and his government obviously think they will get away with anything… that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property”.

The group said the protest might be “the largest public gathering in Czech history”, as organisers expect 400,000 to 600,000 demonstrators.

Although trust in the media is low – about 30 percent to 33 percent according to the latest Reuters Institute Digital News Report – public service journalism is among the most trusted news sources in the country, with Czech Television the most-watched broadcaster across several age groups.

The proposed media reform has attracted international attention: the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have all criticised it.
